title: Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams
description: Before his potential Premier League debut for Fulham, BBC Sport looks at the role international football has played in the development of players like Shea Charles.
fullText:
On an August afternoon at Queen Ethelburga's College in York eight years ago, Michael O'Neill could never have known he was about to set eyes upon two players who would go on to become two of his most important Northern Ireland internationals.

It was then that Shea Charles, who has just become NI's most expensive-ever player at the age of 22, and Isaac Price both donned a Northern Ireland shirt for the first time against Leeds United's Under-16s in a friendly.

The duo played as part of a Club NI side - the academy for Northern Ireland at the time - alongside the likes of Liverpool's Conor Bradley and Portsmouth's Terry Devlin.

It was the first step along an international pathway that would see the pair win senior caps as teenagers under O'Neill before they had established themselves at their clubs. Both are now among the first names on the manager's teamsheet.

In the summer window, Charles became the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer when he joined Premier League side Fulham for £30m from Southampton, who he had joined after leaving Manchester City in 2023.

"You could see straight away there was a player there," said O'Neill as he recalled the first time he watched Charles in 2018.

"I suppose that's one of the biggest pleasures we've had with this team because we've known these boys from such a young age."

Charles' rise to NI's most expensive footballer

Dallas backs Charles to thrive at Fulham

As the examples of Charles and his younger brother, Pierce, show, eligibility is key for a nation with a playing pool as small as Northern Ireland.

Sometimes players are scouted, sometimes the parents or agents of players approach the Irish FA, or clubs can alert the association to eligible players.

Sometimes, however, it is a case of being in the right place at the right time.

Joe Shields, who was head of youth recruitment at Manchester City at the time, got to know the Charles family and knew the brothers would be eligible through their mother, Mary, who comes from Northern Ireland.

After watching Shea progress, Shields contacted Andy Cousins, who was also working at City with emerging talent and with the Irish FA, and recommended that it would be good for his development to get involved in the pathway with Northern Ireland.

From there, Cousins introduced O'Neill to the Charles and Price families ahead of their debuts for the Club NI side.

While O'Neill says he was "being polite and saying hello", it also served a bigger purpose. For an up and coming player like Charles, it left a lasting impression.

"It was really cool for us, to be able to see that the senior manager had that interest in the youth team," said midfielder Charles, who has won 35 caps since making his NI debut in March 2023.

"It was really good to see that he does look at those younger age groups and for boys who maybe have a chance to come through.

"It really helped me get to know the boys, the coaches, the whole set-up and eventually going on my first senior camp and making my debut. It was really special and shows that the pathway was really important."

O'Neill says it is important for him to see the next generation of talent long before they get on the fringes of the senior team, and that the work of Andy Waterworth, director of elite player development, and his staff gives him an opportunity to be in the thick of things.

"I think we're really good at that as a small association," he said.

"With the time frame at that age, it can go quite quickly so there's lads I'm seeing in our academy and I may well be the manager that gives that player his debut."

Cousins, who said Charles "didn't have a worry in the world" at City and "just loved playing football", believes that O'Neill's work with the players at a young age allows him to trust them at senior level, which may not happen at other associations.

"It's allowed him to believe in them and put them on the pitch young and early," said Cousins, who now works as head of scouting at Chelsea alongside Shields, who is co-sporting director at Stamford Bridge.

"I think he worries less about the physical elements, and if he thinks they're going to be a really good player long term, it's about getting them in quickly to try and be at that level."

O'Neill says there are two threads to developing Northern Ireland's playing pool, through domestic-based players and those recruited through eligibility.

There are the success stories of Charles and Price, who came through at Everton before establishing himself at senior level with Standard Liege and West Brom.

But O'Neill adds that if a club releases a player or if their future is uncertain, that the JD Academy - the successor to Club NI - offers stability to help them continue to develop as footballers.

O'Neill pointed to the stories of Dan Ballard and Pierce Charles, who were released by Arsenal and Manchester City respectively, but were still selected by Northern Ireland's youth teams to continue their development.

Now, Ballard is a key player for Sunderland - alongside fellow NI defender Trai Hume - and this summer Charles re-joined Manchester City from Sheffield Wednesday before going on loan to Queen's Park Rangers.

"Their futures were very much in the balance. Pierce was released from Man City at 16, but we don't release him from Northern Ireland.

"It's very important to keep the boys involved as much as we can and try and help and support them when those difficult situations arise."

Shea Charles said the story of his brother was "really important" and it was positive for his development to stay involved with Northern Ireland.

"When Pierce left City, he always had those [Northern Ireland underage] games to play in.

"He always had a spot in those teams and was still able to show what he can do at that high level. I feel that can be the same for so many lads."

O'Neill highlighted the example of Ethan Galbraith, who won his first cap as an 18-year-old in 2019 when he was at Manchester United but only broke into the NI team with more regularity when he was 23 and working his way back up the football ladder with Leyton Orient.

With that time and patience, he is now an integral part of O'Neill's squad and earned a move to Stoke City from Swansea in the summer window.

"You can see the potential in all the young players, but their careers never go in an upward straight line all the time," O'Neill added.

"We never write young players off. We understand that at times they may have difficult times at their clubs, but that's natural. It's a competitive environment."

Despite having smaller resource compared to larger nations, O'Neill believes the IFA's scouting team "doesn't miss very much" when it comes to eligibility.

"We're constantly working at it and we're having conversations with various lads who are at different stages of their careers as well.

"I wouldn't ask a young player to do an international transfer unless I thought they genuinely had a chance to come and be a senior international. I think that's very important."

The second strand is with domestic-based players within Northern Ireland.

Of O'Neill's current squad, players like Trai Hume, Conor Bradley, Ethan Galbraith and Ruairi McConville are all graduates from the pathway.

With the next generation, Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham are examples of getting senior Northern Ireland experience while still featuring at underage level for Arsenal and Everton respectively.

Both players have been in the JD Academy and featured for Irish Premiership side Linfield before they made the move to England.

Charles says that while it is a different pathway than the English club system, the benefit of training and playing together has been beneficial for his team-mates.

"The boys talk about how it was really good for them," he said.

"I'm sure it was a bit different to England, but the end goal was always the same to get to the senior squad, so credit to them."

He adds the fact that, no matter where their football journey started, that they have all come through the underage ranks together has been beneficial at senior level.

"I feel like you can see it on the pitch, with the way we play, and how we talk to each other and congratulate each other.

"When we get a bad result, you can see the way we get around each other. It's a really great group."

Before Club NI was formed, there was a community programme but the full JD Academy, as it is now known, allows the most promising young footballers in Northern Ireland to participate in a residential programme at Campbell College, as well as the benefits that come with playing international football at a young age such as nutrition and strength and conditioning.

For O'Neill, it has been one of the "biggest pluses" since he took over as manager for the first time in 2012, saying the academy has done a "phenomenal job".

"I think we have something which a lot of associations are quite jealous of," he said.

"If you're in a big country, the clubs develop the players because they've got the resources to do it, but our clubs can't do that.

"Not every player in the academy is going to go and be a professional player or will play for Northern Ireland at senior international level, but it is giving them a really good opportunity at a critical time in their development path."

While the Championship is a strong league with consistently challenging opposition, playing international football has allowed Charles to play - and hold his own - against some of the best players of the world.

In the past three years, he has faced Rodri for Spain just before they won the European Championships, Germany's Florain Wirtz, Sandro Tonali for Italy and France's midfield pairing of Aurelien Tchouameni and Adrien Rabiot.

On each occasion Charles held his own - particularly against Italy, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch against Tonali and Nicolo Barella.

On Monday night, the 22-year-old could make his Fulham debut against Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, a potential second Premier League appearance coming three years after his debut under Pep Guardiola at City.

It could be a full circle moment for Charles, as he will be reunited with Cousins and Shields, who played a role in the development of the likes of current Chelsea midfielders Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Romeo Lavia, who came through at City alongside Fulham's new recruit.

"It's much easier to benchmark players when you can say that you've played against players from the Premier League or certainly the top five leagues in Europe," said Cousins.

"Especially where the Premier League is so demanding physically, to see people performing well at that level, it's much easier to trust that and to be able to sign a player.

"I think Shea will be absolutely no problem at all, as he's shown in his performances against those big teams he has played against in the last two years."

Charles agrees and says facing the world's best players has helped him prepare for the Premier League.

"To be in that Premier League environment and hopefully to make my Fulham debut on Monday would just be incredible," Charles said.

"It'll be really cool playing the best players in the world every week.

"I look forward to playing with Northern Ireland and being able to experience those games, even if it's a friendly like the Spain or France games.

"It's does prepare you for what the best players are like, so I'm really looking forward to it."

title: Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve
description: BBC Sport spends a day in Wales' pre-season camp, watching players put through their paces ahead of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Sweat is pouring off Alisha Joyce and Georgia Evans as they emerge exhausted from the spin bike chamber at Wales' training base.

They collapse to the floor fighting for breath as head coach Sean Lynn gives them an encouraging tap on the back.

Next door in the gym Maisie Davies changes the playlist to "It's my birthday" while the forwards go about completing their sets in search of personal bests.

And out on the artificial pitch, Ashley Beck is putting the backs through their paces, with uncapped Amy Williams catching the eye.

This is just a glimpse of life in Wales' camp and for the players three weeks of pre-season pain is almost over.

But for Lynn and the other coaches the hard work continues as they must whittle down the squad for next month's WXV Global Series.

Neumann back in Wales' extended WXV training squad

New-look Wales end losing streak with Barbarians win

Wales kick-off their campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on 18 September before hosting USA on 26 September. They will then head out to Japan for two further Tests on 23 and 31 October.

All three opponents are ranked above 12th-placed Wales, who have lost their last nine competitive fixtures.

And despite a welcome victory over Barbarians in June, Lynn's side know they are still lacking in a number of areas, notably fitness.

It is a key focus for strength and conditioning coach Gareth Harris who is out on the main pitch encouraging the players through an intense set of interval runs.

Keira Bevan is rigged with a social media microphone as she races her opposite number to a marked cone.

"We need to work harder," Harris said.

"We know where we are from a physical perspective and it is about moving that dial forward. A lot of the girls are pretty sore, but that's okay, it's all in the plan."

The 46-strong extended squad has been in camp since 3 August and trained through soaring temperatures, but Harris - who linked up with Wales before last summer's Rugby World Cup - says the attitude has been "exceptional".

"You really see the girls going 'this is important for us'," Harris said.

"We want to be better. We want to be the best team we can be. We don't just want to turn up to the international stage, we want to dominate games.

"There's ownership of the work that they're doing and ownership of our standards and how we elevate those standards and accountability to each person.

"Everybody is going 'this is what I expect of you', which is perfect for us.

"I think we'll see a different Wales this time round."

Harris' optimism is echoed by forwards coach Steve Salvin who has come up to the vantage point of the barn balcony.

He clearly feels at home here having joined Lynn's backroom staff on a permanent basis with Ashley Beck in the summer.

"The four of us [coaches] were thrown together a little bit for the Six Nations, firefighting would be the wrong way to put it but obviously we were working in silos to get things sorted. Now we can be much more cohesive and collective around the way we go about doing things," Salvin said.

"We feel like there's growth in our set piece, our attack, our defence, we're essentially trying to cover all bases.

"During the Six Nations we performed reasonably well for probably 50 to 60 minutes, so one of the things we really need to go after for this series of games is performing for 80 minutes.

"If we do that, we'll give ourselves a much better chance of coming out the right side of the results."

Wales have only tasted success twice since Lynn took over in March 2025, the aforementioned Barbarians game and the first Test against Australia last summer.

But the autumn series will be seen as a major opportunity to get some wins on the board and climb back up the world rankings, where Wales were as high as sixth just three years ago.

And with the new-look WXV feeding into 2029 Rugby World Cup qualification - and a first ever Women's British and Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next September - there is plenty at stake for this group of pre-season players.

title: Russell impresses as Norris shines - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Dutch Grand Prix.
fullText:
Lando Norris won his second race in a row in the final race at the Dutch Grand Prix before it drops off the Formula 1 calendar.

George Russell's win in the sprint race on Saturday, combined with his third-placed finish on Sunday, means he is now level on points with Lewis Hamilton, who he held off to seal a spot on the podium.

Mercedes swapped their two drivers late in the race with Antonelli sealing second place. Further down the order, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc put the pressure on Hamilton late on but could not leapfrog his team-mate into fourth.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in the Netherlands.

Dutch Grand Prix: Recap and reaction as polesitter Norris wins in Zandvoort

Norris beats Antonelli to claim final Dutch GP win

A brilliant response after losing out to Russell and Leclerc in the sprint. Took pole when it mattered and had the pace and patience to chase Antonelli down before reclaiming the lead and controlling the remainder of the race.

His mistake in sprint qualifying damaged the floor and prevented this from being an almost faultless weekend. But he topped practice, recovered to fourth in the sprint, qualified third and produced two superb starts on Sunday before eventually losing out to Norris.

Probably the most complete weekend of anyone even if he didn't win the main event. Sprint pole, a commanding sprint victory, second in the grand prix grid and a podium on Sunday after spending much of the race soaking up pressure from both Ferraris.

A strong weekend without ever quite hitting the heights of the three ahead. Beat Leclerc in both qualifying and the grand prix and pushed Russell hard for the podium, although seventh in both sprint qualifying and the sprint keeps the score down.

One of the stars of Saturday, qualifying third for the sprint before passing Norris for second with an excellent drive on the soft tyre. Sunday's sixth on the grid was disappointing by comparison but he raced aggressively and remained in the podium fight until the end.

Never quite looked as comfortable as Norris. Fifth in the sprint and fourth in qualifying were respectable, but he lost places to both Ferraris during a difficult grand prix in which slow pit stops did him no favours either.

An excellent return to Red Bull in difficult circumstances. Improved throughout the weekend, qualified only a tenth behind Verstappen and brought the car home seventh, although the 10-second yellow-flag penalty was an unnecessary blemish.

His sprint was ruined by a power problem but Sunday more than made up for it. Starting 13th and finishing eighth was a very good recovery and another useful points haul for Audi.

A dreadful Saturday left him starting only 18th after also struggling in the sprint. But he turned that around impressively on Sunday to climb into the points and give Aston Martin something to celebrate.

A very solid weekend from start to finish. Scored in both the sprint and grand prix, reached eighth in sprint qualifying and narrowly missed Q3 for Sunday's race - pretty much maximising what Alpine had available.

Thrown back into a race seat at short notice and looked increasingly comfortable as the weekend went on. Just missed the points in 11th and was only a fraction away from Gasly in qualifying after months without racing in Formula 1.

The raw pace was very good - 10th in both qualifying sessions was another impressive showing from the rookie. But failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags and having to serve a drive-through effectively ended his hopes of points on Sunday.

Quick throughout Saturday and put Audi ninth on the grid for the grand prix. His opening-lap spin dropped him towards the back, though, and turned what had looked like another points opportunity into a recovery drive.

Showed reasonable pace but never looked quite capable of joining Gasly in the points fight. The yellow-flag penalty on Sunday made an already difficult race even harder.

A weekend in which almost nothing went right. Problems delayed his sprint, he qualified last for the grand prix and then started from the pit lane before finishing two laps down.

Trouble from the very first practice session, where his excursions damaged the Williams floor, and things never really improved. Starting 17th was poor and the late collision with Albon, for which he was penalised, capped a miserable weekend.

Williams simply wasn't competitive around Zandvoort and Albon spent the weekend in the lower reaches of the order. His retirement wasn't really of his own making after the late contact with Sainz, who was penalised for the collision.

Again comfortably ahead of Perez in the grand prix grid but Cadillac remained rooted towards the back. His race eventually ended with a hydraulic problem, leaving little opportunity to improve on a difficult weekend.

Quiet but had the better of Haas team-mate Bearman throughout qualifying and the sprint. His grand prix ended through a car problem rather than driver error, so there wasn't much more he could have done on Sunday.

Aston Martin's improved result came entirely from the other side of the garage. Stroll did beat Alonso in the sprint but qualified behind him for the grand prix before damage eventually forced his retirement.

A difficult weekend before Sunday had even begun, with Bearman out-qualified by Ocon in both formats. His grand prix was then effectively over before it restarted when the Haas stopped with a technical problem on the formation lap.

Red Bull was clearly not giving Verstappen the machinery to fight the leading cars and sixth in the sprint and seventh in qualifying appeared about the limit. But crashing out on the opening lap of his home grand prix was a major mistake and has to heavily outweigh the decent work he had done beforehand.

title: Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBC
description:
Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms
The millions who subscribe to the content creator Simon Squibb’s social media channels are usually delivered tips and hacks on how to turn their dream business idea into reality. But they were recently presented with something completely different.
In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms

The millions who But they were recently presented with something completely different.

In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.

Squibb is one of many major UK content creators outraged by a proposal included in a government paper earlier in the summer that would boost content from traditional broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 in the all-powerful algorithms of YouTube and TikTok.

The idea has been pushed collectively by public service broadcasters as a way of boosting trusted material and preserving distinctly British content.

Ministers want to help them survive in a world in which audiences are ditching traditional TV for digital platforms. They prefer a voluntary deal with digital platforms, but have pointed to using legislation if necessary.

Video-sharing platforms and streaming services accounted for 74% of all video time for audiences aged 16-24 in 2024-25, and 69% for 25-34s. YouTube is the most-watched service for children aged four to 15, accounting for 28% of their video viewing.

But the measure has slowly but surely been causing anger and disbelief among content creators, who see it as shifting the goalposts to allow bigger players to stay on top. If the broadcasters go up the algorithm, they reason content creators will be pushed down.

They have been holding private meetings, putting out emergency videos and urging viewers and fellow creators to speak out before the government’s consultation ends at the end of the month, featuring dramatic warnings about “the end of YouTube”.

Squibb and others have even raised comparisons with authoritarian state control. “Russia pushes its channels that it believes the people should watch,” he said.

“I just think it’s a very bad thing to push. Trust has to be earned. If the BBC is selected as one of the trusted sources, does that also mean that Dragons’ Den is going to get prominent coverage over my education and business content? You have to let the public decide.”

Ben Ebbrell, whose Sorted Food channel started as a small project among friends and now has 15 million viewers tuning in each month, said the idea would undermine 16 years of investment in building an audience, a period in which the TV world ignored the growing popularity of YouTube, he said.

“At first, the TV world almost looked down upon content creators, but it’s completely flipped now, where we feel like we’ve got the stardust.

“It was just quite a shock when they said almost that they didn’t want to start playing the game, they wanted to move goalposts – or possibly even running off the pitch with a ball and a bit of a sulk … it’s kind of embarrassing.”

Jade Beason, a creator with 310,000 YouTube subscribers who has worked with traditional broadcasters on their digital content, said they should concentrate instead on making content that works for digital platforms – something the BBC and others are trying to do.

“I don’t think it’s going to get them the results that they need and I think it’s going to disrupt creators in the process,” she said. “To me, it just feels like you’re pushing the queue, you’re jumping ahead.

“[Traditional broadcasters] don’t need more help for people to find them … people aren’t struggling to find TV news, they know where it is. They’re choosing not to watch it. That’s the challenge we should be focusing on.”

Grace Andrews, a content creator who helped set up the Diary of a CEO podcast, is among those coordinating the pushback against the idea and rounding up responses before the end of the month. YouTube has also been encouraging creators to respond.

“Now obviously [traditional broadcasters] are scrambling for eyeballs and instead of adapting to that world, they’re trying to legislate their way back into it,” she said. “Nobody who actually understands why people watch what they watch in 2026 was in the room when this document was created.

“I don’t want misinformation on my feeds either, but I don’t think this is the solution. Social media works because people are choosing what they see. That’s the entire mechanic. The second that becomes something enforced instead of something they picked, they don’t trust it any more.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “We want to ensure that content from public service media providers such as the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and others is easily discoverable on video-sharing platforms, like YouTube, and we have urged the industry to come together and move quickly on voluntary solutions.

“We do not see this as a zero-sum game between traditional broadcasters, content creators and other video platforms. We want to create an environment where PSM [public service media] providers, high-quality news providers and content creators can all thrive.”

title: Could Brooks be Crusaders' next Scottish sensation?
description: BBC Sport NI considers whether Adam Brooks can be Crusaders' next top Scottish striker after his hat-trick against Portadown on Saturday.
fullText:
It was always going to be difficult for Crusaders to find a replacement for the prolific Fraser Bryden, who left the club after one season to join League Two side Chesterfield earlier this summer.

Bryden had come in to take over as the Crues' main goal threat from fellow Scot Kieran Offord, who is now at Linfield after a dazzling half-season on loan at Seaview.

The 22-year-old hit the ground running, with 23 goals in his one and only season in north Belfast helping them to maintain their place in the top flight.

That inevitable led to interest from across the water and Bryden duly left for England, with many wondering how Declan Caddell could replace him.

The answer has come from within and in the form of yet another Scotsman.

Step forward Adam Brooks, whose hat-trick helped Crusaders to beat 10-man Portadown 3-2 in an entertaining game at Seaview on Saturday.

"It was nice to get a hat-trick today, but to be fair I could have had five so there's always room for improvement," Brooks told BBC Sport NI.

"I'm still learning and this is such a competitive league as Portadown showed today even when they went down to 10 men.

"It's been a good start to the season I've got to just keep working hard and stay grounded."

Brooks arrived in the same window as Bryden, joining on a two-year-deal from Queen of the South.

He showed glimpses of his talent last season, playing alongside Bryden up top, or off the wing in a front three alongside the big striker and the pacy Elliot Dunlop.

The 22-year-old contributed eight goals but his form dipped after Christmas just like many of those in black and red as they battled relegation.

With Bryden gone and no direct replacement signed, Brooks was tasked with playing through the middle and providing the focal point the Crues desperately needed.

He was quiet against Cliftonville in the opening day defeat, failed to score in their win against Ballymena last weekend, before bursting into life against the Ports at Seaview.

Brooks showed a real striker's instinct to poke home the opener from Kurtis Forsythe's cross on 11 minutes.

He then drifted between two defenders to latch onto the impressive Owen Wardell's delivery and guide the ball beyond Aaron McCarey on 32 minutes.

The young striker completed his hat-trick, the first scored in the Irish Premiership this season, early in the second half, showing great composure to round McCarey and slot home after capitalising on a slack back pass from Jack Scott.

Those goals will no doubt give Brooks confidence and Caddell will hope the young striker can, like Bryden and Offord before him, show that ruthless streak on a more consistent basis.

"Adam's first two goal were typical of him, he's a predator in the box," said Crusaders boss Declan Caddell.

"We maybe didn't see the best of him last year as I used him out left when we didn't get the best out of him, but we have seen that in pre-season and the first three games.

"He was exceptional today and his hat-trick was well-deserved. I told him he keeps making those moves the goals will come. Thankfully he got three today and could have had more, but I'm delighted for him."

It was a big win for the Crues, who were cruising but then, as they did on so many occasions last season, conceded sloppy goals to allow the Ports a route back into the game.

They defended resolutely after Eamon Fyfe netted a second for the Ports as they made it back-to-back home wins, staying true to Caddell's words that they will look to make Seaview a fortress this year after suffering too many home losses last campaign.

It was another tough day at the office for the returning David Jeffrey, who has now lost his opening three games as Portadown manager.

The Ports were left to rue some poor defending for the Crues' first two goals that left them with a mountain to climb.

That only got steeper when Finn Flanagan was shown two yellow cards for two rash challenges as he was given his marching orders in the first half.

They rallied well in the early part of the second half with goals from Baris Altintop and Fyfe, but Scott's poor back pass allowed Brooks to nip in for the third and they could not find a crucial third which would have secured an unlikely point.

Those were the first two goals the Ports had managed to score this season after narrow defeats against Carrick Rangers and Dungannon Swifts in which they failed to find the back of the net.

"It's thin lines and fine margins," Jeffrey said of his side's start to the season.

"In all of the three games we've played, we should have got something out of them. We have much to ponder and we have much to praise.

"I knew it was a sizeable job when I took it on, we brought in quite a number of players but we will keep working as hard as we can and keep remembering the principles we base everything on and go forward positively."

Jeffrey's side face a tough run of fixtures now as they take on Coleraine, Cliftonville, Larne and Linfield in their next four.

It is hard to see where from those four games their first points of the season will come if they do not tidy up defensively.

title: Fab Four and Fleming on the phone - England's first-Test takeaways
description: Have England improved or were Pakistan really poor? BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt analyses the first-Test talking points from Headingley.
fullText:
England's crushing victory over Pakistan was the ideal start to Joe Root's second reign as Test captain.

The home side could not have wished for a more straightforward beginning to a new era as they look to move on from the chaos of the past year.

England's innings win comes with the context of a desperate performance from Pakistan, so any judgements on progress should be reserved for now.

Still, Headingley taught us some things. Here are the takeaways.

England are rebuilding their bowling attack for two reasons.

First, the retirement of Ben Stokes has robbed them not only of inspiration, but of balance.

Secondly, Stokes has followed Stuart Broad, James Anderson, Chris Woakes and, most likely, Mark Wood out of the door. That is 1,871 Test wickets lost in less than three years.

The first stab at a post-Stokes team included four frontline seamers – Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson – supported by the part-time off-breaks of Dan Lawrence.

In helpful conditions, it could not have gone better for England. Robinson and Tongue took eight wickets apiece, while Archer and Atkinson improved after a rusty first innings when they struggled to adapt following a month playing in The Hundred. Lawrence bowled only one over in the match.

Clearly, there will be times when England need a frontline spinner, but there is no consistently Test-class spinner in the country right now.

There is an argument to be made that England should continue to stack their attack with seamers because they are the best bowlers – Root said they "don't know how good they could be".

The likes of Sam Cook and Brydon Carse wait in the wings to step in or provide different skills if necessary, meaning England have a large squad of pacemen to choose from.

A trip to Bangladesh in February will mean England have to find some spin. For now, they should stay in the fast lane.

'Plug him in as attack leader' - England-Pakistan player ratings

It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root

Jordan Cox has waited a long time for a proper opportunity in Test cricket. Now that it has finally arrived, the Essex batter looks at home at the highest level.

Deputising for the injured Jacob Bethell at number three, Cox impressed with an assured 73. He showed patience and sound judgement, though still had the range of strokes to push the scoring along at a healthy rate without taking risks.

Admittedly, the Pakistan attack Cox faced was far from the most fearsome in Test cricket. None of their seamers had the pace to test his ticker against the short ball.

But, occasionally, players come along and appear instantly suited to Test cricket. Cox seems to fit into that bracket.

His blemish was missing out on the really big score that would have made it impossible for the selectors to leave him out when Bethell returns. Cox potentially has four more innings in this series to make himself undroppable.

If the 25-year-old does demand a place in the XI for the December tour of South Africa and beyond, it leaves England with a dilemma.

Is opener Emilio Gay vulnerable? Bethell is now England's opener in one-day cricket, while Cox opened for Kent at the beginning of his first-class career.

Cox can also keep wicket. Might he put pressure on Jamie Smith? Speaking of whom…

Smith was one of the players who most noticeably wilted under the pressure and scrutiny of the Ashes tour.

He was not helped by a lack of attention to his wicketkeeping in training. Whether it was because a threadbare backroom team was overworked, or England's overall attitude was not good enough, Smith was rarely seen doing the hard yards with the gloves on.

There has been a change this summer. Since joining the coaching staff, former England women's wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor has worked closely with Smith, who has also been able to do more wicketkeeping training with his county Surrey since recovering from a finger injury.

Another circumstance was an injury to Surrey's regular keeper Ben Foakes, one of the best glovemen in the world. It gave Smith three consecutive games behind the stumps in the County Championship in the early part of the season.

The result has been a definite improvement in Smith's keeping for England. It's not as if the 26-year-old ever looked out of place behind the stumps in Test cricket, but he has shown off a greater range of skills this summer, particularly standing up to the fast-medium of Robinson.

At one point, in the third Test against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, Smith even stood up to the pacey Archer.

Not all progress is linear. Smith's Test batting average has dipped below 40 and he needs to avoid developing a habit for maddening modes of dismissal.

The man who somehow got out to a Marnus Labuschagne bouncer in Sydney tamely holed out for 25 on Friday morning when there was an opportunity for a much bigger contribution.

If Cox or Lawrence fill their batting boots this summer, then England's top-order will become congested. Smith must ensure he does not become vulnerable.

Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, is not here. Brendon McCullum's replacement is not due to arrive in the UK until September, by which time the Pakistan series could be over.

Fleming was appointed last month, yet will not take charge of England in a Test until South Africa at Christmas.

The delay has not fully been explained, apart from perhaps a desire to give Fleming a break after almost two decades with Chennai Super Kings.

You will have your own opinions on that one. Being in charge of an Indian Premier League team is intense, but CSK's last match was on 21 May, seven months before England's first Test against the Proteas. Could Fleming, now with one of the biggest jobs in coaching, not have been part of a month-long series against Pakistan?

Either way, Root revealed the New Zealander had been in daily contact during the Headingley Test. "It's been great to have him on the end of the phone," said the captain.

Fleming's influence is not immediately obvious, simply because England were not tested in Leeds.

Should things get more difficult in the remaining two Tests, or if a crucial selection decision needs to be made, perhaps vital input will come from the Flemphone.

'I fear for them' - pundits lament 'desperate times' for Pakistan

A win is a win for England, much needed after only two in their previous 10. However, they should have been better than two wins in 10, and the dismal nature of Pakistan's performance means Root's men can only take limited encouragement from their week in Leeds.

Nothing went right for Pakistan, from the moment captain Babar Azam was ruled out with a thumb injury. Their batting was brittle, their bowling scattergun and their fielding shoddy.

Babar's team beat West Indies in Trinidad earlier this month to earn a 1-1 series draw, yet that was Pakistan's first Test win away from home in more than three years.

They are heavily reliant on winning Tests on spinning pitches, which is why they switched to worn tracks on England's last visit to Pakistan in 2024. When pace bowling becomes the dominant weapon, Pakistan have neither the bowlers nor batters to thrive in the conditions.

Now they head to Lord's, where not one over of spin was bowled in England's shootout win over New Zealand in June.

The surface at the home of cricket could be much different this time around, or a sporty pitch could act as a leveller between the two teams.

Still, the smart money is on another England victory to complete their first series win against anyone in almost two years.

title: The 20 most expensive transfers of the summer (so far)
description: From Morgan Rogers to Ismael Saibari, BBC Sport lists the 20 biggest transfers of the summer so far.
fullText:
Premier League clubs have already spent more than £2bn this summer - but the biggest deals of the transfer window stretch across the globe.

Transfer records, World Cup standouts and unexpected departures, here are the 20 most expensive deals worldwide this summer... so far.

Based on fees reported by the BBC and correct as of 13:00 BST on 21 August 2026. Potential add-ons mentioned separately where applicable.

Bayern signed Morocco attacker Saibari on a deal running until 2031 after a standout season with PSV.

The 25-year-old was named Eredivisie player of the year after scoring 15 goals and providing eight assists in 27 league appearances, before netting three times for Morocco at the 2026 World Cup.

Brighton invested heavily for 19-year-old Croatia defender Vuskovic after an impressive loan spell at Hamburg, where he scored six Bundesliga goals and was named in the team of the season. The deal came after Spurs had paid Brighton £52m for Jan Paul van Hecke.

Italy international Palestra, who was Serie A's defender of the year last season, became manager Xabi Alonso's first signing at Chelsea.

The arrival of the attacking right-back, 21, could offer an early indication of how Alonso plans to structure his new side.

Manchester United paid £48m for Brazil midfielder Santos, who was the first permanent signing under head coach Michael Carrick.

The 22-year-old started only 13 Premier League games last season but is viewed as a long-term addition to United's midfield.

Santos ready to replace 'legend' Casemiro

Villa made Manzambi their most expensive signing, with the initial fee potentially rising further through add-ons.

The 20-year-old was the Europa League's young player of the season after Freiburg's run to the final - where they were beaten by Villa - before contributing three goals and two assists for Switzerland at the World Cup.

Left-back Cucurella publicly criticised Chelsea's hierarchy towards the end of last season and has moved back to his native Spain.

The 28-year-old, who previously played for Barcelona, was part of the Spain squad who won the World Cup this summer.

Van Hecke is reunited with his former Brighton boss Roberto de Zerbi after Tottenham paid £52m for the Netherlands defender.

He started 36 Premier League games last season and led top-flight centre-backs for pressured ball carries.

Chelsea eventually agreed a £52m deal for Lacroix after negotiations with Palace stretched beyond the World Cup.

The centre-back arrives having helped Palace win the Conference League, and made three appearances for France at this summer's tournament.

Dutch midfielder Reijnders leaves Manchester City after one season in England, joining Brendan Rodgers at Saudi Pro League side Al-Qadsiah.

City recouped £52m for the 28-year-old who registered six goals and seven assists in 47 appearances last term.

Summerville opted for a move to Saudi Arabia despite reported interest from Manchester United and Roma.

The Netherlands winger scored seven goals and supplied five assists for relegated West Ham last season, before adding two goals and two assists for his nation at the World Cup.

Liverpool agreed Jacquet's move in January, with the France Under-21 defender recovering from a shoulder injury in time for the new season.

The 21-year-old joins a Reds defence which is being reshaped under new boss Andoni Iraola.

Ramos, 25, became Ruben Amorim's first signing as Milan manager and the Italian club's record purchase.

The Portugal striker leaves PSG having scored 45 goals in 131 appearances across three seasons in France.

Rodri leaves City as one of the defining players of their recent era, having been central to their control in midfield and build-up play.

The Ballon d'Or winner and Spain captain, 30, was also one of the Premier League's most reliable ball-progressors and passers, making his exit a huge tactical loss as well as a major sale.

Gordon signed for Barcelona after a 17-goal season for Newcastle, including 10 in 12 Champions League appearances.

The England winger, 25, also registered a goal and three assists at the World Cup before completing his move to Spain.

Guimaraes, 28, said he wanted a new challenge after leaving Newcastle for Premier League champions Arsenal on a four-year deal.

The Brazil midfielder scored nine Premier League goals last season before finishing the World Cup with four assists in five matches.

Tottenham broke their transfer record to sign Fernandes after just one season at West Ham.

The 21-year-old Portugal midfielder made 36 league appearances, scoring three goals and providing four assists, while also winning 54 tackles.

Spurs soon broke that record again to bring 26-year-old Tonali to north London for an initial £92.5m, with add-ons potentially taking the deal to £100m.

The Italy midfielder said a conversation with compatriot De Zerbi played a major part in convincing him to join.

Real Madrid won the race for Diomande after interest from Liverpool and Paris St-Germain, in a deal which could be worth £120m including add-ons.

The 19-year-old Ivory Coast winger arrives after being named Bundesliga young player of the season, having recorded 12 goals and eight assists, and impressing at the World Cup.

Manchester City broke their transfer record to sign Anderson shortly after the England midfielder returned from the World Cup.

The 23-year-old played in all 38 Premier League games for Forest last season and described City as "winners - the sort of team I want to be a part of".

He was briefly the most expensive British footballer ever, before being surpassed by...

England attacking midfielder Rogers joined Chelsea from Villa for £117m - and pipped Anderson as the most expensive British player in history.

The 23-year-old joins Alonso's side on a six-year deal, having recorded 10 goals and six assists in 37 league appearances last season.

title: Speed-dating, sharks & Hunted - unique pre-season tales from WSL 2
description: BBC Sport looks into some of the unique ways Women's Super League 2 clubs have been preparing during pre-season.
fullText:
Pre-season is a time for building up fitness and embedding new players but in many cases in the Women's Super League 2, it can be an opportunity to have some fun.

With the WSL 2 season kicking off on 4 September, clubs have been busy in the summer with team bonding exercises.

There have been a number of unique team bonding exercises from clubs, while players have enjoyed dipping their toe into activities outside of football.

BBC Sport found out what some of the clubs have been up to...

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Several clubs have been abroad this summer for the start of their pre-season camps, including Nottingham Forest, who were in Canada.

While on a day off, the players visited a wildlife centre and posted photos on social media with some of the animals.

Manager Tom Mallinson also set up a speed-dating activity for the squad to get to know their new signings.

Paired with a team-mate, the task was to say what they appreciated about each other and to learn about their strengths.

"It was really wholesome because we had a different partner each time. The questions were like: 'what does your partner bring to the team?'" said Forest captain Georgia Brougham.

"It made people feel valued. I think that was a moment where everyone really felt together on the trip.

"One of the girls said that she felt like she gained a sister in me. She's Swedish and obviously she's been away from home but she said she feels safe and she can just be herself. It wasn't forced, so it was nice."

Meanwhile, Sheffield United spent a day playing 'Hunted' - a real-life version of the Channel 4 reality television series.

The aim of the game was for team-mates to work together to avoid being caught by those chasing them.

"I'm not really sure what goes on to be honest! We just kind of ran around after each other in the woods," said Sheffield United's Joy Ralph.

"We did it somewhere in the peak district. It's very similar to the TV show. It was fun!"

Elsewhere, goalkeeper Fran Stenson was trying to get to know Sunderland following her move from Southampton this summer.

She was exploring with team-mates along the coast and recalled one encounter with a shark - or so she thought.

"We've been to a few places down by the beach. We went there once and there was dolphins. I didn't expect that," said Stenson.

"I first thought it was a shark. I was like: 'no, am I seeing it right?' There were loads of photographers and I thought it was a shark because I saw a larger fin.

"A guy next to me told me to look out [at the sea] because they were all playing and I realised they were dolphins not sharks. That was one of my first days too."

Over at Wolves, they were put through their paces on a trip to the Lake District which some players were worried about...

"There were rumours about whether we were going to have to put mud on our faces because our manager is in the RAF," said goalkeeper Emily Orman.

"Everyone was worried it was going to be quite a military trip in the Lake District! We were abseiling down a waterfall, there was a bit of fitness involved and campfires - more team bonding stuff.

"But some people were concerned about their skin care routine."

Aside from the team bonding activities, pre-season has been a time for some players to pursue other hobbies outside of football.

Goalkeeper Orman, who joined Wolves on loan from London City Lionesses this summer, has been hooked on video games.

"My boyfriend's kind of indoctrinated me into playing video games because it was his smart way of him getting away with it," said Orman.

"He got me a new computer and was like: 'oh look at this'. He's plagued me with that addiction."

Orman has also been developing her passion for documentary making, which grew while she recovered from a wrist injury last season.

During her time on the sidelines she did some stints as a co-commentator and started to explore roles within the media, creating a new YouTube channel.

"I'm really passionate about trying to do some documentaries in the future," said Orman.

"At the moment I'm just trying to get used to being in front of a camera, filming and editing with just general vlogs. In the future, I'd love to explore women in sport.

"I love Louis Theroux and Stacey Dooley. I would love to learn more. I think that's why I enjoyed the commentary. I really enjoy context.

"Football is another way you can work with so many different people from different countries and in the same team. I enjoy that."

title: What does Heggebo's deception ban mean for football?
description: BBC Sport explores the fallout from the decision to ban West Brom striker Aune Heggebo for two matches for "successfully deceiving a match official".
fullText:
It is 0-0 between Norwich City and West Bromwich Albion with 15 minutes remaining in the opening game of the season at Carrow Road.

Baggies forward Jimmy Jay-Morgan crosses it into Norwich's six-yard box at pace, flying by the outstretched hand of Canaries keeper Vladan Kovacevic and into the path of Albion striker Aune Heggebo.

The Norwegian jumps, seemingly trying to guide it in with his foot but it hits his hand instead and flies into the net.

Did he mean to handball it? Hard to tell at the speed it all happened.

Norwich players protest, but referee Tim Robinson and his assistants did not see it and the goal is given.

West Brom lead 1-0 in the Championship match. Morgan doubles the lead before Mathias Kvistgaarden scores a 90th-minute consolation for the hosts.

In a league without Video Assistant Referees (VAR), apart from the lingering unhappiness at the decision which contributed to West Brom's 2-1 win, that is normally the end of it.

But after the game something unusual happened.

Heggebo became the first player to be charged by the Football Association with "deception of a match official", a little known rule first brought in 2017-18., external

Then on Thursday he was banned for two matches.

Little detail, reasoning or context has been given beyond a factual statement announcing the ban from the Football Association., external

Now attention is turning to what precedent might have been set.

If you gain from something that may well have been accidental – West Brom insist it was – should you own up?

BBC Sport explores the fallout from this decision.

West Brom's Heggebo banned for 'handball goal'

Absence of VAR in Championship is 'crazy' - Clement

Heggebo was charged with misconduct, contrary to FA Rule E3.1, by the Football Association on Tuesday.

In his defence, West Brom argued that the ball took a deflection off the goalkeeper before making contact with Heggebo's hand.

The Baggies claim it affected the ball's trajectory and left the player with "less than 0.1 of a second" to react.

Given the accidental nature of the handball, the club argued, it could not reasonably be viewed as a deliberate act of deception.

Since the ban was announced on Thursday, West Brom have said they are going to write to the FA requesting clarification on how a player is reasonably expected to react should similar circumstances arise in the future.

Retrospective disciplinary action has previously been taken against players guilty of simulation.

According to English football's governing body, the FA can take retrospective disciplinary action in situations where a match official may have been deceived.

This process is not for debatable decisions, but only where there is overwhelming evidence to indicate that a player intentionally deceived a match official.

However, West Brom believe that this charge is the first of its kind in English football following a rule change two years ago.

The incident reopened the debate over the use of Video Assistant Referees (VAR) in the Championship.

VAR is used in all matches in the Premier League but EFL clubs have blocked its introduction to date.

In April, clubs in the second tier of English football turned down the chance to introduce a version of the VAR system for 2026-27.

BBC Sport understands the idea is closed for the foreseeable future and is unlikely to be resurrected by the clubs in a year's time - so no opportunity to review incidents like this shortly after they happen.

Heggebo, who joined West Brom from Norwegian side SK Brann for an undisclosed fee in 2025, will miss his team's next two games at home to Burnley on Sunday (12:00 BST) and away at Newcastle United in the second round of the Carabao Cup next Wednesday (19:45 BST).

West Brom issued a statement backing their player after the two-game ban was announced.

"We remain steadfast in our support of Aune, whose character and integrity have been evident throughout his time at The Hawthorns," it read.

Speaking to BBC WM, West Brom fan Alistair said the club had been treated harshly by the FA.

"It's not our fault the referee didn't see it.

"What is he supposed to do? Go to the referee and say: 'you know what ref, I've handballed that and then get a rollocking off his gaffer after the match?'.

"It's not Thierry Henry against the Republic of Ireland or Diego Maradona against England."

Former Norwich City striker Chris Sutton, however, told BBC Sport that the outcome will "make players think twice about punching the ball into the back of the net."

"There's an argument that you can blame the officials for missing it - I get that," added Sutton.

"But the player successfully deceived the officials and we shouldn't be rewarding or encouraging that.

"That's why it's right the player has been banned."

Former West Brom and Ajax midfielder Richard Sneekes disagreed, telling BBC WM:

"I just can't see how the FA can do this. It's absolute nonsense. Where are they going to draw a line?"

Heggebo's ban has been welcomed by Martin Cassidy, chief executive of Ref Support UK, external - a charity committed to the support of referees.

He wants the rule implemented more throughout the 2026-27 season as he believes it will help stamp out incidents of players deceiving the officials.

Cassidy said he had no sympathy for West Brom or the player and cited an incident in 1997 when Liverpool striker Robbie Fowler won a penalty against Arsenal - and then told the referee to overturn his decision., external

"Heggebo should have owned up," added Cassidy. "Deceiving the officials is not welcome and this is a really positive step.

"This rule has been around for a while. They have never really used it as much as they could.

"For me, this is a really positive step forward that could change the game for the good."

title: Inverness dream big after dark days - watch Partick Thistle match on BBC
description: Inverness Caledonian Thistle have been through a lot in 12 months and now harbour ambitions of returning to the top flight. Watch their Friday BBC Scotland live match with Partick Thistle.
fullText:
In fewer than 12 months, Inverness Caledonian Thistle have gone from being a Scottish League 1club in administration to potential dark horses for a return to the Premiership.

Scotland great James McFadden tipped them as one of the teams to watch this season during BBC Scotland's first live Championship match of the season.

Some managers baulk at the pressure such predictions can bring, but Caley Thistle boss Scott Kellacher is loving it before Friday's home match with Partick Thistle in front of the BBC Scotland cameras.

And Kellacher said: "I thought to myself, 'good on you, Faddy Boy!' I'll give him his due, he's a man that's always positive and I love it.

"You want people to come to games and you want them to be excited. You want them to look forward to the game and it's not going to be boring this-and-that.

"That's what you get with us. We want to be an entertaining, attacking-type team. Get you on the edge of your seat.

"When Faddy said that, I thought 'that's a real nice comment'."

Kellacher's side have had a solid if unspectacular return to the Championship so far. They have played two of last season's Premiership play-off contenders, Dunfermline Athletic and Arbroath – with both matches ending 0-0.

However, the fact Inverness Caledonian Thistle are still a going concern is in itself a minor miracle after the financial issues that threatened the very future of the club.

Despite the burden of a five-point penalty last season for going into administration, Kellacher, assisted by Billy Mckay, steered the club to the League 1 title after local businessman Alan Savage took the reins behind the scenes.

Kellacher has nothing but praise for the way Savage has brought the club back from the brink.

"I actually couldn't speak any higher of the man," said Kellacher of Savage. "He's just got a special way about him in terms of how he goes about everything.

"He allows me and Billy to get on with the job. We have a wee meeting once a week to make sure everything is all right, do we need anything? If so, what do we need, can we help? It's never any problems, it's solutions.

"Everybody at the football club is so grateful for him coming in and giving everyone a new lease of life."

Inverness CT v Partick Thistle on Sportscene

Kellacher is well aware his side face a major test of their credentials on Friday evening against a Partick Thistle team that look like potential favourites to win the division.

Mark Wilson's Glasgow Jags have won both their league matches so far, without conceding a goal. They also only narrowly lost 1-0 away to Premiership side Hibs in the League Cup.

Caley Thistle fared less well in the capital on Sunday, albeit they were 2-1 up against Hearts at Tynecastle before capitulating to a 6-2 defeat.

So, is there really a chance of the Faddy fairytale coming true for Caley Thistle this season and a double promotion?

Kellacher said: "I said it to the players on Sunday, I say it to the fans - be a dreamer. Why not? What have you got to lose?

"I was always impressed with John McGlynn's model, how he's managed to do it with the [Falkirk] squad he had. He managed to do it, which was incredible.

"If we ever had the chance of doing that, I think it would be a phenomenal achievement from where we've come from and the dark days.

"I'll never get carried away. I try and keep my feet on the ground.

"But I say to the players, go and dream on doing something like that. Why not? What's stopping you from being the best you can be and be up there at the end of the season?"

title: Headlining on TikTok & targeting KO record - Serrano eyes history
description: Seven-division champion Amanda Serrano talks to BBC Sport about fighting on TikTok, going for the women's boxing knockout record and retirement plans.
fullText:
After 17 years, 54 fights and world titles across seven weight classes, Amanda Serrano is still making history. This time, she's coming for your algorithm too.

The Puerto Rican defends her WBA and WBO featherweight titles against Argentina's Lucrecia Manzur on Friday in California, in the first world championship boxing event to be streamed live on TikTok.

A 33rd stoppage triumph, in what would be Serrano's 50th professional victory, would give her the most knockout wins in women's boxing history, eclipsing pioneer Christy Martin.

"That's what gets me up in the morning, working hard, training hard," Serrano tells BBC Sport.

"I always set myself little goals. Because if your dreams don't scare you, they're not big enough.

"To tie was an honour, but now we have to break it. I don't like being tied."

The bout is Serrano's penultimate appearance in an illustrious career, and another chance for the 37-year-old to add to a legacy that has transformed women's boxing.

"This is the social media era. We're in 2026. A lot of these young generations are constantly on the phone," she adds.

"They're always scrolling, scrolling and scrolling. So what better place [than TikTok]?"

Briton Hennessy in talks for undisputed title fight

Shields eyes Price after dominant middleweight return

When Serrano turned professional in 2009, Facebook and MySpace were the digital frontier. She only joined TikTok six months ago but has quickly embraced the platform.

"I do TikTok Lives every day at seven o'clock. I've grown a big fan base there - I call them my TikTok family," she says. "

"I do giveaways, give tickets away for my fights. They came to California, they came to El Paso. You do battles, you meet so many people. I'm excited to make history."

Headlining on TikTok feels natural for a champion who has seized every non-traditional stage to push women's boxing into the spotlight.

Serrano shared 30 brutal rounds across three historic bouts with Katie Taylor - twice on Netflix - and alongside the Irishwoman and Claressa Shields, has driven the sport's commercial boom.

She credits Most Valuable Promotions co-founders Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul with helping transform both her career and the wider sport, saying she was close to retirement before joining the promotion.

"When I leave this sport, I want to be considered a game-changer," Serrano adds.

Having matched Martin's 32 stoppages, Serrano believes returning to two-minute rounds for this 12-round bout could deliver the finish.

"We all want a knockout," she says. "With the two minutes, I get to give it my all. It's so much higher pace than three minutes. I can just give everything."

Beyond Friday, the curtain is coming down. Serrano has mapped out a solitary farewell in Puerto Rico, targeted for later this year or early 2027.

While former undisputed super-bantamweight champion Ellie Scotney has moved up to featherweight and is targeting Serrano, the reigning champion remains focused on her exit strategy.

She has already begun guiding the next generation under MVP, managing talents like Krista Rosado and Alexis Chaparro.

"I love Ellie as a person, and as a fighter she's great, but right now I'm concentrating on this fight," Serrano says.

"Seventeen years, I've accomplished what I wanted. Now it's time to enjoy the sport from the other side, watching them."

Fittingly, long-time rival Taylor is also preparing for her own farewell against Flora Pili at Dublin's Croke Park on 5 September.

"I already fought my dream opponent three times," Serrano smiles. "Retiring so close together, we might share the Hall of Fame together.

"I wouldn't be prouder than to share that moment with Katie Taylor. She's a great champion and a great human being."
