At Chelsea, Maresca mainly used a man-to-man press high up the pitch. In pre-season we have seen City defend high up the pitch but in a more zonal fashion – something City did last season.

City's starting shape here has looked like a 4-2-4 before players spring to press certain opponents when the moment is right.

Reflecting on how the game has changed in pre-season, Maresca said: "Usually the team that was defending found the solution by going man-to-man. Now the teams that try to build up are trying to find solutions against man-to-man. I don't know when but there is going to be a bit of change."

And his change in defensive approach appears to be trying to ensure his side are ready for teams who are preparing to play against man-to-man presses more often.

In pre-season, this has been the weakest part of City's system with players, often in midfield or at full-back, having to cover large distances, leaving gaps in their defensive shape.

Like with any defensive approach that involves an element of pressing, this improves with time, as players better understand the press, as well as when physical condition improves.

But this was a part of the game Guardiola tweaked often last season, struggling to land on something he was completely happy with.

There is benefit in Maresca's hire following Guardiola because it provides a sense of familiarity, particularly in the team's identity and their principles.

The 3-2-2-3 shape was the shape City won the treble with. The high and wide wingers, given multiple one-against-one situations per game, and the focus on cut-backs were seen in City's centurion season.

Meanwhile, the use of full-backs moving infield and attacking the box were obvious in City's 2025-26 campaign – as was their 4-2-4 defensive shape.

Maresca's system is its own but interestingly there are references to City's last decade as the club look to begin a new chapter.

title: When do the major European leagues start and what are the big stories?
description: BBC Sport looks at the big stories in Europe heading into the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
The start of the Premier League may still be a week off, but in Europe the new season is already getting under way.

With La Liga kicking off this weekend and Ligue 1, Serie A and the Bundesliga soon to follow, there are plenty of storylines to look forward to this season.

BBC Sport rounds up the best and looks ahead to what should be an enthralling campaign on the continent.

First La Liga match: Alaves v Getafe, Saturday 15 August, 18:30 (BST)

Jose Mourinho returning to Real Madrid 13 years after his first spell as manager ended was a reunion nobody saw coming.

Many expected Real to dominate La Liga and the Champions League when they signed Kylian Mbappe in 2024, and while he has impressed, the team as a whole has not gelled.

Last season Real looked like two teams on the same pitch - a group of four superstar attackers, and a fragile defensive unit left vulnerable to counter-attacks.

New signings Marc Cucurella, Ibrahima Konate, Denzel Dumfries and Bernardo Silva should help shore things up, while Yan Diomande could provide even more excitement in the final third.

Vinicius Junior has also recently agreed a new deal after being linked with Arsenal.

Some suggest a veteran Mourinho has had his day - can he manage the egos of Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius after his previous time in charge at the Bernabeu ended following dressing room disquiet, and does the Special One still possess the tactical acumen to seriously challenge Barcelona?

Hansi Flick's side were not as formidable last season as in 2024-25, but a squad full of Spanish World Cup winners are still favourites to win a third consecutive league title.

Replacing the goals of Robert Lewandowski will not be easy, but reinforcements have arrived in the shape of Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi.

As usual, Atletico Madrid will look to muscle their way into the top two, with Villarreal and Real Betis heading up the best of the rest.

After fighting their way up from the third tier, Malaga will look to avoid the drop with a budget but tightknit squad - they have been under judicial administration since 2020.

There will be tears in Valencia as Los Che play their final campaign at the iconic Mestalla stadium, but who knows if Uefa Conference League runners-up Rayo Vallecano will be able to play any home games at all.

The regional government of Madrid has stripped the club of its license to host matches at its rented Vallecas stadium due to the dilapidated state of the facilities.

La Liga to inspect Celta Vigo's pitch after fungus outbreak

New season, new boss - will Alexander-Arnold be key figure at Real Madrid?

First Serie A matches: Udinese v Como & Inter Milan v Monza, Saturday 22 August, 17:30 (BST)

Inter Milan are fancied to defend their Serie A crown, albeit partly because few teams look equipped to challenge them.

Napoli, AC Milan, Atalanta and Lazio all have new managers, while Juventus and Milan are both under pressure after missing out on the top four last term.

While the absence of Champions League football could aid their title bids, playing Thursday nights in the Europa League could hinder them.

How Ruben Amorim gets on at San Siro will be particularly interesting for Manchester United fans.

Napoli, whose two most recent title defences have fallen disappointingly flat, will hope Max Allegri can rediscover his knack for winning.

Como were the big story of last season, but can Cesc Fabregas' side replicate their league success while navigating a debut Champions League campaign?

They face a race against time to complete improvements at their idyllic lakeside stadium if they are to host European games.

Given the recent struggles of the Italian national team, Fabregas has pledged to try and bring through more young Italian players. Will others follow suit?

Roma did well to finish third last season after a rocky start, and have backed manager Gian Piero Gasperini in the transfer market. Can they kick on and win a first Scudetto since 2001?

Mourners line streets of Milan for legend Baresi's funeral

Defender Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer

First Bundesliga match: Bayern Munich v VfB Stuttgart, Friday 28 August, 19:30 (BST)

The age-old question is as relevant as ever after Vincent Kompany's side cruised to a domestic double last season while playing some truly scintillating football.

Harry Kane is 33 now but is showing no signs of slowing down - the England captain has scored 98 goals in 94 Bundesliga games and has broken countless records.

While questions may be asked of 40-year-old goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and his unconvincing backline, Bayern's devastating firepower of Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Diaz, plus the addition of Morocco international Ismael Saibari, means they should easily outscore their opponents.

Borussia Dortmund, RB Leipzig and Bayer Leverkusen are all capable of launching title challenges, but tend to come unstuck against stubborn mid-table sides.

Elsewhere, fallen giants Schalke 04 are looking to re-establish themselves as a top flight side after three years away. Their promotion heralds the return of one of the fiercest derbies in world football - the Revier derby against Dortmund.

Elversberg were playing in the regionalised fourth tier as recently as 2021-22, but secured promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time in their history to complete a fairytale rise.

With a population of about 13,000, Spiesen-Elversberg will be the smallest town to be represented in the Bundesliga. The odds are stacked against them.

Kane set for talks with Bayern Munich over new deal

Ex-Man City striker Dzeko, 40, pens new Schalke deal

First Ligue 1 match: Marseille v Strasbourg, Friday 21 August, 19:45 (BST)

It is hard to see anything other than Paris St-Germain winning Ligue 1 for the 13th time in 15 seasons, especially off the back of back-to-back Champions League triumphs.

That said, Luis Enrique's side can be got at - last season they lost six league games, two more than in the previous two campaigns combined.

PSG have added attacking midfielder Maghnes Akliouche from Monaco and Aston Villa left-back Lucas Digne to their star-studded squad this summer, but could end up selling wingers Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye amid interest from Liverpool.

Monaco (2016-17) and Lille (2020-21) are the two most recent sides to topple the Parisians, but neither looks equipped to do so again.

Financial difficulties have limited traditional heavyweights Marseille in the transfer market, with more key players set to follow Mason Greenwood out of the club.

Will Still (Auxerre) and Liam Rosenior (Paris FC) are back in the league after ill-fated managerial spells in England, while former Brazil full-back Felipe Luis has been installed as Monaco boss.

Lens were PSG's closest challengers last season, but may need time to bed-in new manager Dino Toppmoller. Lille, who finished third, face a similar situation with Davide Ancelotti.

Strasbourg have been a team on the up in recent years, but after losing manager Rosenior and then Gary O'Neil to the Premier League, face another restart under the relatively inexperienced Hugo Oliveira.

After losing the spine of the team that reached the Uefa Conference League semi-finals last season, the Alsace side have suffered some heavy defeats in pre-season.

Pogba expected to have Monaco contract terminated

Digne completes move to PSG from Aston Villa

Plenty of big names have joined Turkish clubs in recent years, but Mohamed Salah signing for Trabzonspor came as a surprise.

After leaving Liverpool at the end of his contract, Salah decided to join the 2021-22 Super Lig champions rather than one of Turkey's big three - Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas. He'll be remembered as a hero if he can deliver a title at the first time of asking.

In the Netherlands, PSV Eindhoven are looking to win a fourth successive Eredivisie title.

Ajax and Feyenoord are looking to bounce back from disappointing campaigns having since appointed new managers - Spaniard Michel at Ajax and former Netherlands captain Giovanni van Bronckhorst in Rotterdam.

Porto are looking to successfully defend a Primeira Liga title for the first time since 2013, but will surely be challenged by Clasico rivals Benfica, now under the management of Marco Silva.

Sporting CP are looking to reclaim the title after winning it in 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The Eredivisie and Primeira Liga are already under way, while the Turkish Super Lig begins on Friday, 14 August with Galatasaray v Corum (19:30 BST).

title: The main contenders to replace Rodri at Man City
description: As a move for Manchester City midfielder Rodri looks increasingly likely, BBC Sport takes a look at the options to replace him.
fullText:
Enzo Maresca has been in his new job as Manchester City boss just six weeks, but already he may be on the cusp of having to make a tough decision.

With Rodri heavily linked with a move back to his native Spain, Maresca's first challenge may well be to find a replacement for a World Cup-winning captain and Ballon d'Or winner.

Rodri, 30, is in the final year of his contract and City have already rejected a £38.5m bid from Barcelona following interest from Real Madrid.

After helping the Blues win the Treble in 2023 then triumphing at the Euros with Spain a year later, an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed Rodri's dominance somewhat.

But he showed glimpses of his brilliance for City last season before returning to the Rodri of old as he captained Spain to World Cup success in the summer.

His stock is high, and a move from Manchester after seven seasons with the club would leave a huge hole for Maresca to fill.

So who are the leading candidates to step into the Spaniard's boots?

Age: 18 Country: Morocco Club: Lille

Talk of City signing Bouaddi has been rumbling all summer, and the club have reportedly held talks with the Moroccan,, external who would cost an estimated £85m.

Bouaddi is said to be keen on the move.

The teenager impressed at this summer's World Cup after a starring role in Lille's Champions League victory over Real Madrid in 2024 announced him on the big stage.

Bouaddi functions as a deep-lying conductor - much in the same vein as Rodri - and would complement summer signing Elliot Anderson, who is more of a box-to-box midfielder.

Taking into account the loss of Bernardo Silva, it is not just Rodri that City are trying to replace and, with 30 Ligue 1 appearances last season, Bouaddi possesses a level of experience beyond his age.

Age: 25 Country: Argentina Club: Chelsea

City have been heavily linked with Fernandez, and he is currently the favoured option for Maresca, who worked with him at Chelsea.

But the London club are expected to stand firm on their £120m valuation - a hefty sum considering City have already spent £116m on Anderson.

Maresca made Fernandez captain at Chelsea in the absence of Reece James. The Italian clearly sees Fernandez as not only a talented player but also a leader, something City would be shorn of should Rodri move on.

No-one has made more Premier League appearances under Maresca than the Argentine, whose attacking intent and runs into the opposition box are attractive.

Fernandez returned to Chelsea training this week after helping Argentina reach the World Cup final, where he was sent off as they lost to Spain.

And Chelsea have set a deadline of 17:00 BST on Friday for any offers for him as they look to bring an end to uncertainty over his future before the season.

The club are said to be willing to fully reintegrate him into the squad and would continue to regard him as a key player.

Fernandez scored 15 goals and provided seven assists in 54 appearances for Chelsea last season. Of the options in this list, he also comes out on top for successful passes, passes into the box and successful passes into the final third.

Age: 22 Country: England Club: Bournemouth

City have explored a potential move for England international Scott this summer.

The 22-year-old has rejected contract offers from the Cherries amid interest from other Premier League teams, though his current deal does not expire until 2028 and the club have expressed their desire to keep him.

Bournemouth rejected a £64m bid from Chelsea for the midfielder last month and made it clear that any further approaches would not be welcomed. Advances from Arsenal have also been knocked back.

Scott's energy and ball-carrying ability suit Maresca's preferred style of play - with a heavy emphasis on possession - while his passes into the box and ability to win duels make him an appealing option.

Age: 27 Country: Argentina Club: Liverpool

Perhaps the most surprising name to be linked with City is Mac Allister, but the Blues have explored a potential move for him.

The Argentine is into the final two years of his contract at Anfield and has been a consistent presence in the Reds' midfield during his time there, though he struggled for form during a troublesome 2025-26 season.

As a Premier League winner, Mac Allister would bring top-flight experience and be a ready-made candidate to slot into City's midfield.

A versatile player, he can play as a holding midfielder or as a more box-to-box option. As the oldest option on this list, Mac Allister would also offer a wealth of experience.

Should Rodri depart, Maresca's side are somewhat lacking in leaders, with club captain Silva and experienced campaigners John Stones and Nathan Ake also leaving.

Maresca is believed to want a homegrown player in the leadership group, which consists of Rodri, Ruben Dias and Erling Haaland.

Despite his outspoken nature, Haaland does not seem suited to Maresca's demands of a captain on the pitch, which leaves Dias as the front-runner for the armband.

"Erling was one of the first to send a message when I joined the club," said Maresca.

"At Leicester and Chelsea I had a rule that when we scored the captain had to come to the bench, not to celebrate, but for instructions. But if he scores, then he can celebrate.

"If Erling is the captain, we have a problem... can you imagine?"

Phil Foden has captained City during pre-season and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma is a vocal presence on the pitch, while defender Marc Guehi skippered former club Crystal Palace.

title: Will West Ham bounce straight back up?
description: BBC Sport analyses the season ahead for West Ham, who will be playing in the Championship for the first time in 14 years.
fullText:
When Declan Rice hoisted the Europa Conference League trophy aloft in 2023, few would have envisaged that West Ham United would be preparing for life in the Championship just three years later.

A first major trophy for 43 years followed a Europa League semi-final the season before and would be backed up by another European quarter-final in 2024.

The Hammers also finished sixth and seventh in the Premier League in 2021 and 2022.

It was an era for the east London club in which relative success had become the norm.

But things can change quickly in football and for the first time in 14 years, West Ham will be playing outside the top flight.

The Irons are the favourites for an instant return to the Premier League, which they achieved in 2011-12, though the English Football League (EFL) can be an unforgiving environment, even for a club boasting the biggest stadium in Championship history.

And with an ownership tug of war playing out behind the scenes, which way will it go for West Ham in the 2026-27 campaign? BBC Sport takes a look.

This is a path well trodden by other big clubs in English football in recent history.

Newcastle United have dealt with adversity with relative ease on the two occasions they have been relegated to the Championship, in 2010 and 2017, and bounced straight back.

Aston Villa dragged themselves back following relegation in 2016, but it took three years, including a 13th-placed finish in their first season in the second tier followed by a play-off final defeat before eventual promotion.

But Leicester City, Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United fans can all attest to just how quickly the situation can spiral once a team is sucked into the EFL grind.

Leicester were Premier League champions 10 years ago. This season they will be playing in League One, just two years after relegation from the top flight.

Blackburn lifted the title in 1995 and enjoyed several European campaigns along the way.

But Rovers were relegated to the Championship in 2012 - and to League One in 2017. They are yet to get out of the EFL.

Similarly in 2005, Leeds were relegated just four years on from a Champions League semi-final and one year after a UEFA Cup campaign.

It would take 16 years and a journey down to the third tier before Leeds played in the Premier League again.

It was Jarrod Bowen who netted the dramatic last-minute winner for West Ham against Fiorentina on that memorable night of European glory in June 2023 to etch his name into the club's history books.

And Bowen committing his future to the club is perhaps better than any summer signing West Ham could have made.

Bowen has been the club's top goalscorer in four of the past five seasons, netting 76 times in 227 games in all competitions.

He has also provided 53 assists and signalled his intent for the current campaign in Saturday's 3-1 victory over Portsmouth in the EFL Cup, scoring one and setting up another.

An England international, a player of his pedigree could prove invaluable.

"It was a no-brainer for me to be here and the vision is clear," said Bowen after confirming he would stay at the London Stadium. "It's the Premier League."

But the 29-year-old is fully aware of the challenge the Championship provides.

"It's 46 tough games, midweek, Saturday, Tuesday, Friday," Bowen said.

"There's going to be disappointment at times, there's going to be a lot of pressure on us to go and win the league straight away.

"That's our aim, but I'm telling you now, it's not going to be as easy as that."

Manager Nuno Espirito Santo agrees.

"Normally when a team drops to the Championship, you have to be the favourite, mainly because our objective is to go back to the Premier League," the 52-year-old told BBC Radio London.

"We realise how hard it's going to be. We're going to have to be resilient, to keep going.

"Tight schedule, very tough competition, a lot of good teams with the same aspirations as ourselves.

"But we are ready for the challenge."

Retention of key personnel is arguably the most important factor for the Hammers in 2026-27.

Nuno's choice to remain is a luxury not every relegated side always has - Burnley start the season with a new boss, Nicky Hayen, and likewise Wolves with Cesar Peixoto.

Nuno has been there and done it before at this level with Wolves, winning the Championship to gain promotion in 2017-18.

"I look at West Ham as being the team that has kept hold of an incredible manager," ex-Nottingham Forest and Ipswich Town defender Luke Chambers told the BBC's 72+ podcast.

"I think it's a massive coup. It's almost like having an £80m signing coming in. He is top, top level."

There is a proverbial elephant in the room at West Ham though, with an ongoing ownership saga.

Relegation made high-profile player departures inevitable.

Midfielder Mateus Fernandes signed for Tottenham for £85m, winger Crysencio Summerville joined Saudi club Al-Hilal in a deal worth £60m and Freddie Potts, who came through the West Ham academy, has gone to Belgian champions Club Brugge.

Those exits, in theory, should allow West Ham to reinvest that money.

But with a £104.2m loss in their most recent accounts, new Squad Cost Rules (SCR) to comply with and Amanda Staveley's co-ownership struggle, it is not as simple as splashing out every penny of that £150m to overhaul the squad.

The situation is complex and likely to drag on for several months into the new season.

A consortium led by Staveley - the former Newcastle United co-owner - has agreed to buy the Gold family's 25% stake in the club.

But current co-chair Daniel Kretinsky has publicly opposed Staveley's deal, and appears to be working hard to keep her from getting a foot in the door.

Nuno insists funding for transfers is not a problem.

"It's not about the money. We don't have too much time, but what we can't afford is mistakes," Nuno said.

"We have to make it right. To avoid mistakes is crucial this year. The player that comes in the door has to have the same purpose and be identified with the mission we have ahead."

Glyn: Boardroom issues, inevitably, filter down to the pitch. With this wrangling going on, how is it possible to plan? Not many incomings, so far, and the uncertainty surrounding ownership will not aid that process.

Dave: The way this board and its advisors are working, I can see us doing a Luton, which is sadly nothing more than they deserve. I have supported this club for 58 years and I can not remember a worse time.

Andy: Recruitment, as ever, will be the problem, and I predict after a standard very slow start, we'll finish 5th, missing out in the play-off final.

Brendan: If West Ham can't begin to iron out their very obvious off-field problems, they won't have a chance in the Championship.

How will relegated trio fare in the Championship?

Fighting relegation & eyeing promotion? Championship set for six-team play-offs

Despite concerns from some supporters, those working in the game still expect West Ham to challenge at the top.

"I don't think they will be a Leicester," said Bromley manager Andy Woodman.

"They're a little bit more stable than Leicester were. If they can get a few early results and get that fan base on board, it could be massive. I think West Ham will be a force to beat this year."

Former Nottingham Forest striker Lyle Taylor also believes West Ham's home support - with 50,000 season tickets sold - could be crucial.

"If the fans decide 'we're behind the team, we're behind the manager, we're going to push them over the line,' then I can see West Ham winning the Championship at a canter," he said.

West Ham's squad will take on a fresh appearance when they visit Burnley in their first Championship game of the season on Sunday.

Centre-back Axel Disasi has returned to Chelsea and Callum Wilson has joined Brentford, while Fernandes, Summerville and Potts are long gone.

Winger Manor Solomon, who scored 10 goals in 39 Championship games to help Leeds United win promotion in 2024-25, has arrived from Tottenham for £5m.

Ex-Brighton defender Joel Veltman, 34, has also joined, while Mexico international Edson Alvarez has returned from a loan spell with Fenerbahce, as have James Ward-Prowse from Burnley and George Earthy from Bristol City.

There is still time for further additions and West Ham already have the core of a competitive team.

Keeping hold of key starters attracting interest, including defender Konstantinos Mavropanos, will also be essential to an immediate return to the top flight.

"We are going to face the pressure, that's our job," goalkeeper Mads Hermansen told BBC Radio London. "We are West Ham, we are the biggest club in the league and we want to show that we are going straight back up."

Strong words from the Dane, even if promotion is unlikely to be a formality. Nothing ever is in the Championship.

title: 'Same players making the same mistakes' - Howey
description: Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.  The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.  "I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.
fullText:
Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.

The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.

"I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.

"And I'm talking missing chances, even though they might be half-chances and some of them were but some of them were more than half-chances.

"When you've got the ball getting drilled into you, make it stick, but it's bouncing off players, and I'm just thinking we used to see that last season. And I know there's been the World Cup, and you have still got time to work on these things - it's not going to improve straight away, it's going to take time. But it was just annoying because it is the same players making the same mistakes again.

"They'll have a little bit of a breather as such, they'll stretch off and do whatever they have to do, but then go again at the weekend with the two games before getting really ready for the start of the season. Only they'll know individually and collectively if they're ready, but whether they're ready or not, it's coming."

title: 'I'd never watched the Olympics' - Evans on gymnastics fame
description: British gymnast Ruby Evans speaks to BBC Sport about how she copes with fame and followers ahead of the 2026 European Artistic Gymastics Championships.
fullText:
Ruby Evans did not appreciate the scale of what she was about to do back in the summer of 2024.

Competing at the Paris Olympics as a 17-year-old catapulted her into the spotlight.

Two years on - with a Commonwealth gold medal, 127,000 Instagram followers and almost two million likes on TikTok - the gymnast is of one of Britain's rising stars.

"I didn't actually think I'd get that many followers after the Olympics," she told BBC Sport.

"Because I was so young, I'd never really watched an Olympics. I didn't actually realise how many people watched the Olympics.

"I remember just opening my phone [after competing] and it wouldn't even turn on, there was just so much going on."

Success has required resilience. Never more so than at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

On the Sunday evening, Evans left the arena in tears after a disappointing sixth in the individual all-around competition.

On Tuesday she returned to earn Wales a historic gold in the floor final..

She said afterwards she'd turned her anger into motivation, with the proud Welsh gymnast claiming her "dragon was absolutely firing" for her gold medal-winning performance.

Despair to delight for Wales' golden girl Evans

'I feel amazing' - gymnast Evans on Olympic selection

Social media attention can bring a dark side.

Female athletes in a range of sports have complained about the abuse they get - from rugby to tennis players.

Evans is no stranger to negative comments - but she refuses to let it affect her.

"It doesn't matter who you are, you're going to get nasty comments," she said.

"But if they're not doing anything better and they can only comment on other people's lives, then you're already winning.

"I know some people will get offended by it and that's obviously OK. I just say never show the person that you're offended because they're going to keep doing it.

In a period of new faces in British gymnastics, 19-year-old Evans is well placed to become the next star of her sport.

At the Paris Olympics, she and her team-mates came agonisingly close to a medal, finishing fourth by 0.2 points in the women's team final.

She followed up her debut Olympics with a silver medal in the floor event at the 2025 World Championships.

After that gold in Glasgow, she is aiming for more success at this week's European Championships in Zagreb, Croatia - which will be live on the BBC from Saturday.

For someone who routinely sails through the air, her feet are firmly on the ground.

She says she is not driven by medals. Improving as a gymnast is her biggest motivation.

But asked if she's targeting gold at the LA 2028 Olympics, she smiles.

"Maybe," she adds. "If I'm good."

For individual success at an Olympics, she will need to showcase two vaults with different entries on to the vault.

So that is her current focus in training.

"Maybe if I get a second vault, I'd have quite a good chance," she added.

"But it's in gear two. It needs to get to gear five."

At the Europeans, Evans and her team are focusing on a strong performance in Sunday's women's team final as that will set them up for October's World Championships - and with it a chance of Olympic qualification.

As ever, there's likely to be a lot of attention on Evans - she's been showing she is someone worth keeping an eye on.

2026 European Artistic Gymnastics Championships

Women's event 13-16 August; men's event 19-23 August

title: Messi's most iconic moments as he ponders retirement
description: As Lionel Messi considers his footballing future following the death of his father, BBC Sport looks back at some of his most iconic moments.
fullText:
Lionel Messi is considering his future in football after the death of his father, Jorge.

The 39-year-old Argentina forward is signed with Inter Miami until 2028.

But, in an emotional tribute to his dad, he hinted at retirement as he said: "I don't know how to carry on. I used to just play football, and now I'm really not sure if I'll carry on doing it for much longer."

He has scored a combined 921 goals for Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Inter Miami and Argentina.

BBC Sport looks at some of the most iconic moments of his remarkable career.

Messi unsure he will play 'much longer' after father's death

A rivalry that changed football

'That's why he's the king' - Messi sets up third World Cup final

Messi's first career hat-trick came in one of the biggest fixtures in football - El Clasico.

At the age of 19, he scored all of Barcelona's goals in a 3-3 draw against rivals Real Madrid on 10 March 2007 - his first at the Camp Nou - including a brilliant last-minute finish after beating a couple of defenders.

This was arguably the moment he became a household name.

Just over a month after that hat-trick, Messi scored a goal he has probably never surpassed in the rest of his glorious career.

It came in a 5-2 win over Getafe in the Copa del Rey semi-final first leg on 18 April 2007.

In a strike with remarkable similarities to compatriot Diego Maradona's (non-handball) effort against England in the 1986 World Cup, Messi picked the ball up in his own half, beat about five defenders, went around the goalkeeper and slotted home.

Ridiculous as it sounds now, back in 2009 some English football fans and journalists questioned whether Messi could do it against English opponents in Europe - having failed to net in 10 Champions League appearances against Premier League sides.

But there were no more doubts when Messi rose highest in the box to head home Xavi's cross in his first Champions League final against Manchester United - and the first game billed as Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo.

Two years later he would score in another final win over Sir Alex Ferguson's men to claim the third of his four Champions League winners' medals.

Messi scored four goals for the first time in his career as he took Arsenal to the cleaners in the 2010 Champions League quarter-final for a 4-1 home-leg win.

The pick of the bunch was his chip over keeper Manuel Almunia to complete his hat-trick.

An honourable mention goes to his five-goal haul two years later against Bayer Leverkusen in a 7-1 last-16 success.

He is the second top scorer in Champions League history with 129, behind Ronaldo.

Messi broke Barcelona's goalscoring record - aged just 24 - in some style with a hat-trick in a 5-3 victory over Granada on 20 March 2012.

He equalled Cesar Rodriguez's 60-year-old record of 232 goals with his first, broke it with his second and extended the record with a third.

A stat so amazing you have to go back to double check to make sure it really happened.

In 2012 Messi hit his 91st goal of the year in Barcelona's 3-1 win at Real Valladolid on 22 December.

It earned him a place in the Guinness Book of Records., external

He netted 79 goals for Barcelona and 12 for Argentina - in a total of 69 games for club and country.

It was enough to earn Messi a then-unprecedented fourth consecutive Ballon d'Or - even though he only won the Copa del Rey in 2012 for all those goals.

This was the second major record Messi broke with a hat-trick.

He hit three in a 5-1 win over Sevilla on 22 November 2014 to become the top scorer in La Liga's history.

Messi equalled Telmo Zarra's 251-goal mark - set in 1955 by the Athletic Club forward - with a free-kick, before breaking it and stretching it with a third.

He ended up on 474 goals, far clear of Ronaldo's 311 for Real Madrid.

All the narratives seemed to come together in Barcelona's 3-2 win at Real Madrid on 23 April 2017.

Messi popped up with an injury-time goal, sweeping home a first-time shot from the edge of the area. It was an El Clasico winner, his 500th Barcelona goal and it sent his side top of the table - although Real would go on to win the league at the end of that season.

For good measure, he pulled out an iconic celebration when he took off his shirt and held it out so the Bernabeu faithful could see his name.

The almost unthinkable happened in August 2021 as Messi left Barcelona on a free transfer.

After 21 years, 672 goals and 35 trophies, he had to leave because the club could not afford to honour the new contract they agreed because of La Liga's salary limit.

In an emotional news conference, a tearful Messi said: "My family and I were convinced we were going to stay here, at home.

"I don't want to leave this club - it's a club I love and this is a moment I didn't expect."

Despite being linked with Manchester City, he joined Paris St-Germain.

On 11 July, 2021, Messi - at the age of 34 - won his first senior international trophy as Argentina beat Brazil 1-0 in the Copa America final at the Maracana.

He was named player of the tournament after scoring four goals.

An emotional Messi fell to the ground as the full-time whistle blew and was thrown in the air by his team-mates as they celebrated.

He won his second Copa America three years later.

It was a triumph and moment that looked like it would never happen, with Messi having previously retired from international football before coming back.

It was always the thing held against him in debates about whether he was the greatest footballer of all time.

Messi scored two goals, and his effort in the 2022 shootout, as Argentina beat France on penalties after a 3-3 draw in the best World Cup final ever.

He was named player of the tournament, having netted seven times - including efforts in each knockout round.

Messi won another two Ballons d'Or after leaving Barcelona - one at Paris St-Germain and one at Inter Miami - to extend his record haul to eight.

His last one came in October 2023 after he won the World Cup and helped his Major League Soccer side lift the Leagues Cup for their first trophy.

"I couldn't imagine having the career I've had and everything I've achieved, the fortune I've had to be part of the best team in history," he said.

"All of them [Ballon d'Or awards] are special for different reasons."

If 2026 was to be his last World Cup, Messi certainly went out in style.

His eight goals in the tournament took him 21 in the World Cup - more than anyone has ever scored, until Mbappe went past that tally to 22 in the Bronze Final defeat by England.

Aged 39, Messi's World Cup may have ended in disappointment - as Argentina lost to Spain in the final - but individually it was another month on football's biggest stage few will forget.

title: Inter Milan close in on £25.6m Djed Spence deal
description: Inter Milan are in advanced talks with Tottenham Hotspur over a deal to sign England full-back Djed Spence for at least £25.6 million (€30m).According to BBC Sport, the 26-year-old has emerged as a...
fullText:
Inter Milan are in advanced talks with Tottenham Hotspur over a deal to sign England full-back Djed Spence for at least £25.6 million (€30m).

According to BBC Sport, the 26-year-old has emerged as a key target for the Serie A champions after enhancing his reputation at the 2026 World Cup, where he made eight appearances for England.

The Guardian has independently reported that negotiations are ongoing over a transfer worth approximately €30m (£25.6m), with Spence keen on a move to Inter. The Italian club are looking for a replacement for Denzel Dumfries, who has joined Real Madrid.

Spence made 23 Premier League starts for Tottenham last season as they narrowly avoided relegation and has established himself as a versatile option capable of playing on either flank.

He joined Spurs from Middlesbrough in July 2022 for a reported £20m and has since made 85 appearances for the club.

Tottenham have already begun exploring potential replacements as the prospect of Spence's departure grows.

Inter's interest comes as they reshape their defensive options under Cristian Chivu, with the England international's ability to operate as a full-back or wing-back making him an attractive option.

Spence's future has become increasingly uncertain despite signing a new contract with Tottenham last season. He is reportedly keen to secure regular first-team football, while Spurs are willing to consider his departure if their valuation is met.

The negotiations are continuing, with Inter increasingly confident of reaching an agreement for the England international.

title: Can Mourinho restore Real Madrid to former glory?
description: Jose Mourinho is back at Real Madrid 13 years after leaving the club. But can the 63-year-old recapture the success of his first spell and deliver trophies at the Bernabeu? BBC Sport speaks to those who know Mourinho and Real Madrid best to assess whether his second stint can be a success.
fullText:
Jose Mourinho left Real Madrid in 2013 as one of the most celebrated managers in world football.

Thirteen years later, the self-proclaimed 'Special One' is back at the Bernabeu, tasked with restoring a club that has had two successive seasons without a trophy.

But Mourinho's return raises an intriguing question.

Is the 63-year-old still capable of reaching the heights of his past, or has Real Madrid's president Florentino Perez turned to a manager whose best days are behind him?

Speaking on the More Than The Score podcast, BBC Sport spoke to those who know Mourinho best to assess whether he can make a success of his second spell with Los Blancos.

Mourinho says he agreed to replace Ferguson at Man Utd

New season, new boss - will Alexander-Arnold be key figure at Real Madrid?

Mourinho has won only one title since he left Madrid, the Premier League during his second stint at Chelsea in 2015. His subsequent spells at Manchester United, Tottenham, Roma, Fenerbahce and Benfica have produced moments of success in cup competitions, but also considerable turbulence.

Spanish football expert Eduardo Alvarez believes Mourinho's appointment came about because club president Perez took inspiration from Carlo Ancelotti's successful second spell at the club.

"I think he's betting on a second stint with Mourinho because Ancelotti was successful during his and it's a very similar case," Alvarez told BBC Sport.

"Ancelotti was coaching Everton, probably not at the top of his game anymore, 60 years old and suddenly, when he went to Real Madrid again, it worked out and he won the Champions League.

"Mourinho falls into the category of Real Madrid not being a manager's club but being a player's club. Even though Mourinho is a very prominent manager, the way he manages is not tactically intense, but more player-intense, which is what I believe Florentino needs."

An iron fist joining a broken team: Inside Mourinho's Real return

What now for Vinicius Jr after Mourinho signs Real Madrid deal?

But there is a former Real president who believes Mourinho will have to change if he is to succeed.

Ramon Calderon, who led the club from 2006 to 2009, has welcomed the appointment, but warned the Portuguese cannot simply recreate the approach of his first spell.

"He's going to need to change the behaviour and the attitude of the players," he told BBC Sport.

"He showed, when he was at Real 13 years ago, a lot of protagonism. He had many problems with clubs, rivals, referees and was always blaming others for the defeats and not taking the responsibility.

"I think he has to gain the respect and trust of the players by persuasion, not by imposition. He has to show them that his methods are the best ones for whole team and not have protagonists."

After leading Inter Milan to a Serie A, Coppa Italia and Champions League Treble in 2009, Mourinho's first Madrid spell then produced a La Liga title, the Copa del Rey and three successive Champions League semi-final appearances.

But it was also marked by fierce rivalries, dressing-room tensions and a highly volatile relationship with the Spanish media.

"I hope he can change," added Calderon. "If he insists on the same mistakes, it will be a problem."

That question of whether Mourinho has changed has also been asked in Portugal, where he spent last season managing Benfica.

Portuguese football journalist Duarte Monteiro believes the answer is no.

He added: "Mourinho didn't change. His character, his personality didn't change. The problem, I think, for him is that the world changed.

"The young players today, the journalists and the environment is different and I think there's not as much openness to embrace him now like maybe there was 20 or 25 years ago, when his character was fresh and new."

Monteiro described Benfica's football last season as "not very sexy", with Mourinho adopting a conservative approach and appearing to have different priorities in domestic and European competition.

There were still highlights, notably a famous 4-2 victory over Real Madrid in the Champions League group phase before they later lost a play-off tie.

But Monteiro said Mourinho's old personality traits remained evident as he added: "He had two or three moments over the season where he was very publicly aggressive towards a group of players.

"Not every player at Benfica was with him last season."

Former Chelsea defender Robert Huth helped Mourinho's side secure back-to-back Premier League titles in 2005 and 2006.

But he admitted: "I was impressed but a bit scared as well.

"When I did interact with him, it was very brutal. Looking back now, it was basically: if you don't perform, you're gone."

Yet Huth said that harsh approach was appropriate for a young player trying to establish himself.

"He was very hard but fair, always honest with his communication with you," he added. "When you weren't playing, you knew exactly why you weren't playing.

"If you had a family problem, or any kind of outside issue that might have an effect on your performance, he was always there for you. He was always a family man. Players developed a really human relationship with him."

Mourinho's greatest strength, he believed, was his ability to convince an entire squad to buy into a common cause and mindset.

That proved key to Chelsea's success under Mourinho, which also included the FA Cup and League Cup.

"He galvanised the squad," said Huth, who also won the Premier League with Leicester City in 2016.

"When you have someone leading like that, you kind of go, 'Yeah, I'm in'.

"His training was pure quality, his preparation was amazing, the level of detail he brought to the club, his mentality, the coaches he brought in - they were all on the same page."

That may be the biggest question Mourinho has to answer, with the Real dressing room containing Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Jr and Jude Bellingham among a collection of elite players.

Mourinho's methods have traditionally relied on establishing strong relationships with key personalities and demanding total commitment.

"I think Bellingham will absolutely love Jose," said Huth. "He will thrive under him."

But he has concerns about Mbappe and Vinicius as he added: "When things don't go their way, things come out in the Press. I don't like that kind of thing.

"Bellingham is that kind of guy that gives everything each game. Jose loves that."

Managing such stars will prove a defining challenge for Mourinho, said Calderon too.

"The dressing room is full of stars, he has a fantastic squad," he added. "But it can be a problem if you don't manage it properly."

In his first managerial role at Porto, Mourinho was desperate to prove himself at the highest level and show his worth.

He took over midway through the 2001-02 season, famously saying he would make them champions the following year.

He delivered, building a team with relatively unknown players but hungry for success. He won the Portuguese title and Uefa Cup in 2003, then retained the league title and won the Champions League in the following season.

Journalist Monteiro admitted that version of Mourinho was impossible to recreate.

"What Mourinho did at Porto was a once-in-a-lifetime job," he said. "The big difference is that back then he needed to prove something.

"Now I think he only needs to prove something to himself - and sometimes that's not good for him."

At 63, Mourinho has nothing left to prove in terms of reputation, but Real Madrid may demand and need something different.

It's not simply the charisma and tactical intelligence that made him a global managerial icon, but the ability to adapt.

Huth said Mourinho still possessed "unbelievable knowledge" of the game, but now needed to convince the current players at Real Madrid to believe in him completely as those at Porto, Chelsea and Inter Milan once did in their quest for more honours.

title: European Championships: Day three schedule & BBC coverage
description: Timetable and BBC coverage times for the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham from 10-16 August.
fullText:
The first European Athletics Championships to be held in Great Britain are under way at Alexander Stadium in Birmingham.

The Championships take place from 10-16 August, with Britain's team of 94 athletes chasing top spot in the medals table.

Among the British stars on show are reigning 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson, Dina Asher-Smith, local boy Matthew Hudson-Smith, Katarina Johnson-Thompson, Amy Hunt, Georgia Hunter Bell and team captain Jake Wightman.

Global stars competing include Sweden's Armand Duplantis, Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen, Greece's Miltiadis Tentoglou, Italy's Marcell Jacobs, Ukraine's Yaroslava Mahuchikh and the Netherlands' Femke Broeders-Bol.

Athletes from 49 nations are competing for 50 gold medals - including a mixed 4x100m relay for the first time - and there are 10 world champions and seven Olympic champions taking part.

The BBC will bring you comprehensive coverage of the championships on BBC One, BBC Two, BBC iPlayer, Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website, the BBC Sport app and the BBC Sport social media channels including YouTube.

Hodgkinson & Asher-Smith in GB squad for Europeans

Sprinter Asher-Smith has won six European golds and two silvers from four championships and could overtake the record of seven golds to become the most successful athlete in the history of the competition.

Two athletes jointly hold that record - Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic (formerly Perkovic) and Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who picked up his seventh title with men's 5,000m victory on the opening night in Birmingham.

Asher-Smith finished sixth in her opening event, the women's 100m, but is expected to compete for two further medals - the women's 200m and either the mixed or women's 4x100m relay.

The 30-year-old could also draw level with fellow sprinter Irena Szewinska of Poland as the most-decorated European athlete of all time. Szewinska won a total of 10 medals from 1966-1978.

Of other current athletes, Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol has five golds and a bronze from just two championships.

Hudson-Smith, who has a stand at Alexander Stadium named after him, has four golds and seven medals in total.

One more medal and he will equal France's Christophe Lamaitre as the championships' most-decorated male athlete of all-time.

A gold medal would also bring him level with Roger Black and Sir Mo Farah as the British men to have won most European titles.

The 31-year-old, who was born in Wolverhampton, competes in the men's 400m final on Wednesday evening and will have a further chance of winning a medal in the men's 4x400m relay on the final day.

Arguably the most-anticipated event for British fans is Hodgkinson's 800m battle with Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol.

Hodgkinson, 24, sat out the Commonwealth Games and comes into the championships after winning the London Diamond League meeting in July.

However, she faces two tough opponents in her quest for another title.

Swiss star Werro, 22, beat Hodgkinson in June and has twice run faster than the reigning Olympic champion this season, edging closer and closer to the 43-year-old world record of one minute 53.28 seconds.

Broeders-Bol, the 26-year-old world 400m hurdles champion, has moved up to 800m and finished just behind Hodgkinson at London Stadium as she makes rapid strides in her new event.

The women's 800m heats took place on Tuesday morning, the semi-finals are on Thursday morning at 12:10 and the final is at 21:45 on Friday, 14 August.

The team behind Hodgkinson's golden rise and the hunt for a world record

Why is the women's 800m record so tough to break?

Hunt is targeting a British record four gold medals at these championships in a bid to become "iconic".

The confident 24-year-old won 100m gold on Monday and is aiming to follow that up by winning the 200m title on Thursday, the women's 4x100m relay on Saturday and the inaugural mixed 4x100m relay on Sunday.

"Yes, I am looking to be iconic," she told BBC Sport. "I want to do what nobody has ever done before.

"I think this is the perfect place to do it. I am an East Midlands girl, and I am from Newark.

"This is the closest I am ever going to get to a home crowd in my entire career."

Team-mate Asher-Smith won three gold medals at the 2018 Europeans in Berlin.

You can watch live coverage of every session on either BBC One or BBC Two as well as iPlayer, the BBC Sport website and the BBC Sport app.

Radio 5 Live and BBC Sounds will be in Birmingham to bring you daily live commentary, while the BBC Sport website and app will feature live text, reports, analysis, video clips and a medal table.

There will also be coverage on BBC Sport's social media platforms, including YouTube.

Gabby Logan and Jeanette Kwakye will present the BBC TV coverage with Steve Cram, Andrew Cotter, Steve Backley, Colin Jackson and Paula Radcliffe commentating on the action.

London 2012 Olympic champions Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill and Greg Rutherford plus Hodgkinson's coach Jenny Meadows will also provide analysis.

title: How will relegated trio fare in the Championship?
description: BBC Sport England looks at how the three relegated sides - West Ham, Burnley and Wolves - will navigate the Championship this season.
fullText:
With their generous parachute payments, it is often expected those who drop out of the Premier League will be the big contenders to shoot straight back up - but that was not the case last season.

Only Ipswich Town returned to the top flight, and while Southampton did make up for a terrible start under boss Will Still, his replacement Tonda Eckert's spying tactics put an end to their hopes of bouncing back.

And then there was Leicester City, who ultimately failed to escape a double relegation just a decade on from lifting the Premier League trophy.

Yes, the Championship is trickier than some might think. Will the three relegated sides - West Ham United, Burnley and Wolverhampton Wanderers - be able to navigate it?

It has been a whopping 14 years since West Ham have been in the second tier but the side have been in steady decline since the high of winning the Europa Conference League in 2023.

In the end, it came down to a close, fascinating scrap between them and fellow top-flight stalwarts Tottenham Hotspur for survival - but four losses in their final five games sealed the Hammers' fate.

Most of the headlines surrounding West Ham this summer had nothing to do with football.

There was a joint BBC Panorama and The Times investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct against West Ham co-owner David Sullivan, which he categorically denies.

This was followed by Vanessa Gold, West Ham's co-chair, confirming her family's plans to sell its shares in the club to a consortium headed by ex-Newcastle United co-owner Amanda Staveley.

However, fellow co-chair Daniel Kretinsky sold just over 2% of his stake in the club to Czech businessman Jakub Havrlant, making it possible for Kretinsky to purchase Gold's shares under the club's pre-emption rights clause, which gives existing shareholders first refusal on available shares.

The whole process around the sale of Gold's shares could take two months, well into the new season.

What will be key to their success?

The retention of captain Jarrod Bowen is a major bonus for the Hammers.

The 29-year-old forward's skillset should prove tricky for most second-tier defenders. He has also got pace and a high work-rate, which should serve him well in a physical league.

Boss Nuno Espirito Santo could also be influential in West Ham's success.

Despite suffering a poor end to last season, notably he is now the only head coach of the relegated trio to have managerial experience in the English Football League.

The Portuguese took charge of Wolves in 2017 and led them to the Championship title in his first season, and his exploits in the Premier League since, particularly at Molineux and Nottingham Forest, will mean there will be plenty of expectation that he can get them promoted the first time of asking.

Not to forget the power of the fans. London Stadium will be the biggest home ground the Championship has ever seen, housing 62,500 people. That is 51,831 more than Lincoln City's Sincil Bank.

What is the expectation this season?

West Ham are the bookmakers' favourites to win the title and their pedigree alone is enough for their fans to have faith in an immediate bounce back.

Off the field though, the headlines surrounding the club have been a cause of concern and it is not unreasonable to believe the uncertainty could take a toll on the players and coaching staff.

The Hammers did impress with a 3-1 victory over Portsmouth in the first round of the EFL Cup though and their opening game against Burnley on Sunday, 16 August (16:00 BST) could be telling as to how their season will unfold. Dazzle again there and their fans will be blowing their bubbles freely.

Burnley have been on the promotion-swiftly-followed-by-relegation rollercoaster for a few seasons now.

They have experienced four promotions to the Premier League under three different managers since 2014 - Sean Dyche, Vincent Kompany and Scott Parker - and three of those promotions, including their past two, ended in an immediate drop back to the second tier.

Last season's Premier League campaign proved to be their toughest season yet, ending with a mere four wins - just 22 points - to their name.

Burnley's former boss Scott Parker left by mutual consent back in April and the timing of appointing his replacement has left many fans concerned.

Wales head coach Craig Bellamy had been heavily linked with the role in June, with the Clarets approaching the Football Association of Wales in a bid to bring the 47-year-old to Turf Moor.

However, it was not to be. Compensation was seemingly no issue but negotiations for Bellamy's backroom staff to join him at Turf Moor were thought to be a point of contention.

In stepped Genk boss Nicky Hayen, an appointment that had some wondering if it was made out of hope rather than meticulous planning.

What will be key to their success?

Recruitment. The Clarets have seen 12 departures so far this summer and will need to rebuild their squad with a team that fits Hayen's style of play.

The Belgian likes to play high-possession football and wants to be direct once in a position to attack, so players who are good on the ball and able to intercept will be high on his wishlist.

New signing Ugo Raghouber fits that profile perfectly - he's a defensive midfielder who is known for breaking up attacks and he's good in the air.

The only other outfield player the Clarets have purchased this summer, forward Lluc Castell, fits the club's preference for the stars of tomorrow since ALK Capital completed their takeover in 2020.

Of the 20 new players they brought to the club ahead of their promotion-winning Championship campaign in 2024-25, 12 were aged 25 or under.

The following season in the Premier League, the Clarets stuck to this model, with seven of their 15 arrivals being 25 or under. Three were over 30, including veteran defender and former England international Kyle Walker.

Castell shows plenty of promise but, at just 19, is still very much in development.

While a younger squad may have struggled to compete at the top level, it's been effective in the second tier - and Walker will be wanting to add a Championship trophy to the overflowing cabinet filled with accolades from his years at Manchester City.

Burnley know how to run a promotion campaign.

They do not tend to linger in the second tier too long and both previous managers that were appointed by owner Alan Pace - Kompany and Parker - won promotion back to the top flight at the first time of asking.

But yo-yoing between the first and second tiers suggests they have an unsustainable model - and this year could be their most perilous yet.

Walker targets instant Burnley top-flight return

Wolves sunk to the bottom of the Premier League under former boss Vitor Pereira after going winless in their opening 10 games of last season.

Things did seem to take a short upswing when Rob Edwards took the reins in November and they finally got their first victory against West Ham in January, but there would be no miracle escape as they finished 20th in the table and 21 points from safety.

The Wolves fans make no secret of their misgivings over the transfer habits of their club.

Whether it was winger Pedro Neto's departure to Chelsea or Manchester United's swoop for forward Matheus Cunha, for years now Wolves have sold their best players for big money and the weakness of their squad during the 2025-26 season suggested it had not been wisely invested back into the team.

Owners Fosun seemed to have turned a corner, though, in this transfer window, bringing in the experience of full-back Kieran Trippier and keeping hold of midfielder Andre, as well as welcoming back the popular figure of striker Raul Jimenez.

However, the goodwill over Jimenez's return quickly faded with the sacking of Edwards days later and his replacement with little-known Portuguese head coach Cesar Peixoto, external.

That change also seemed to stall Wolves' ambitious start to the transfer window.

What will be key to their success?

Peixoto is known in Portugal for his attacking football and how that transfers into the Championship could be key to how well Wolves perform this season.

The 46-year-old is looking to stamp his aggressive but pragmatic identity on to his new side.

A high press could feature often in Wolves' upcoming campaign but he will also be looking for cool heads and smart football.

All of this is just theory though as Peixoto is untested in English football and he has inherited a side that struggled to keep it together under the pressure of the Premier League.

The appointment feels risky - even more so given many fans felt Edwards' arrival last season was intended for life back in the Championship after he took Luton Town to the top flight in 2023.

Trippier and Jimenez, both 35, joined with Edwards in the managerial seat, bringing the much-needed experience Wolves required.

The talent of 18-year-old Mateus Mane was one of the few highlights in a poor Premier League season and undoubtedly fans will be hoping to see more exciting fresh faces signed before the summer transfer window closes.

What is the expectation this season?

Wolves will be hoping lightning strikes twice and that, as with their memorable 2017-18 title-winning season, a mysterious, untested Portuguese manager will lead them to glory.

He may have a lack of experience in English football but there is plenty of it in the dressing room thanks to the new signings and Peixoto's attacking football could inject a little life into a disillusioned Molineux.

The relationship between the fans and Fosun remains frosty though and you have to feel only a strong season will help to repair the damage done over several years of disappointing transfer windows.

It's a new era, the past is the past - Peixoto

title: Who is prospective new Celtic signing Hassan?
description: BBC Scotland takes a look at Egypt winger Haissem Hassan, who seems poised for a move to Scottish champions Celtic.
fullText:
Having burst on to the World Cup stage this summer, breakout star Haissem Hassan now appears bound for Celtic.

The Egypt winger is reportedly set for a medical in Glasgow after Celtic agreed an initial £6m transfer fee, external, that could rise to £9m, with Real Oviedo.

It would end a saga and take Celtic's haul of new recruits this summer to three as the hugely-important Champions League play-off with LASK looms large.

Martin O'Neill has stated his desire for quality over quantity in replenishing a squad that has lost more than a dozen players since last season's league and Scottish Cup double success.

So, why have Celtic zoned in on Hassan and what will he bring?

Celtic hope to complete Hassan deal soon - Scottish gossip

'Celtic fans are going to fall in love with him' - Hogh makes his mark

Hassan played just 126 minutes at this summer's World Cup, but it was enough to send his reputation rocketing.

He did not feature in any of Egypt's Group G matches with head coach Hossam Hassan later revealing it was down to a paperwork delay in registering the former France youth international.

The 24-year-old was finally unleashed as a second-half substitute in Egypt's last-32 penalty shootout win over Australia - before delivering a standout performance against Lionel Messi's Argentina.

A left-footer deployed on the right flank, Hassan started the last-16 match and set up Mostafa Zico's goal, skipping past Enzo Fernandez before drilling in a precise delivery to help put Egypt 2-0 up.

However, it was the Egypt's infamous disallowed goal in their agonising 3-2 defeat by the defending champions that showcased Hassan's direct running and dynamic dribbling qualities.

Bursting forward from the right-back area, he evaded two challenges in a 60-yard run before threading a pass through for Mohamed Salah, who teed up Zico.

Across his two World Cup performances, Hassan registered nine dribble attempts at a rate of 6.4 per 90 minutes.

If Celtic had hoped to keep their interest in the winger under the radar, that prospect was blown out of the water with his impact on football's biggest stage.

Hassan was born in France and represented Les Bleus at Under-17 and Under-18 level before switching allegiances and making his senior international debut for Egypt, his father's birthplace, earlier this year.

He started his club career in central France at Chateauroux, featuring initially for their B team and then the senior team in the lower leagues.

A move to Spain's Villarreal followed in 2020 where he turned out for their B team, then went on loan to Mirandes before returning to the Yellow Submarine for his first taste of top-flight football in La Liga.

Another loan, to Sporting Gijon, followed and Hassan stayed in the second tier before a move to Oviedo in 2024.

He helped the club win promotion in his first season, scoring four goals and setting up three, but the going was far tougher in La Liga last term.

Hassan contributed three assists and couldn't muster a goal in 37 appearances, 20 of those from the start, as Oviedo finished bottom to immediately drop back down.

His xG (expected goals) of 0.15 last season hints at a paucity of clear chances in a team that were the lowest scorers in the division by a distance.

Kasper Hogh is an out and-out-striker, while fellow new arrival Camilo Duran, who can play wide or through the middle, is left-footed but has been deployed on the right wing in Celtic's opening two games of the season.

That right-wing berth would likely become Hassan's, with Duran shifting over to the left in place of Yang Hyun-jun.

Manager O'Neill has also hinted at playing two up top, which would mean a Hogh-Duran front pairing and Hassan providing ammunition on the right with Yang on the left.

That would give Celtic's attack a similar look to that of the Gordon Strachan era, when Shunsuke Nakamura and either Aiden McGeady or Shaun Maloney operated as inverted wingers, supporting a central pair of strikers - typically Jan Vennegoor of Hesselink with Giorgios Samaras or Scott McDonald.

Celtic's link-up play really stretched Kilmarnock in the 5-1 weekend win, with hat-trick hero Hogh coming deep and going long to combine with his team-mates.

The wingers and midfielders got into advanced positions throughout, with three different players providing assists for Hogh's goals.

Adding Hassan would offer Celtic a fresh and exciting option in a fluid attack.

title: Can Lawson keep seat for 2027 season? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
fullText:
Formula 1 cars will be back on track next week when the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort takes place from 21-23 August.

In the meantime, you can get your F1 fix as our correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

As a Kiwi, I'm biased - but clearly Liam Lawson's been performing at Racing Bulls so far this year, and he's currently 'best of the rest' in the driver standings. Thoughts on his future in F1, particularly before the 2027 season? - Isabella

Lawson is having a strong season.

Given Racing Bulls have the fifth quickest car on average this season, and Lawson is considerably the more experienced of their two drivers, 'best of the rest' in the championship behind the drivers from the top four teams is exactly where he should be.

However, Lawson's issue - in terms of prolonging his career in F1 - is recent history, and his current team-mate.

Arvid Lindblad is a rookie this year, but he is already proving pretty much a match for Lawson. As team principal Alan Permane puts it, the team have "two quick guys" who are "incredibly close" in performance.

Lindblad is trailing in the championship by 20 points, yes, but on pure pace there is little to choose between them.

Lawson leads the qualifying head-to-head 6-5 at races where a fair comparison can be made but, on average speed, Lindblad is actually slightly ahead - by 0.017secs.

That's impressive for a rookie in this context.

Equally, Isack Hadjar was more impressive than Lawson in 2025 - hence Red Bull's decision to promote him in favour of Yuki Tsunoda for this season.

In terms of whether he is a candidate for a move up the grid, Lawson will not find it easy to recover his reputation from the two poor races he had alongside Max Verstappen at the start of 2025, after which Red Bull took the decision to demote him back to Racing Bulls and swap him with Tsunoda.

Once there, Lawson was pretty comfortably beaten by Hadjar.

As for this season and the future, Permane points out the goal of him and his team is to "develop drivers" for Red Bull.

If Red Bull were still run by the old regime of Helmut Marko and Christian Horner, there would be no hope of Lawson getting another chance in the senior team.

The modus operandi of the new leadership, of Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies and soon-to-be head of the young driver programme Gwen Lagrue, and how they view Lawson in all this context, remains to be seen.

Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season

Listen: Chequered Flag Extra - mid-term report

How does F1/the FIA decide where to have sprint races? Silverstone - with a big crowd in every day - was great this year but other races this season didn't look like they had full stands on the Friday and Saturday. - Phil

The location of the sprint events is ultimately decided by Formula 1 as the commercial rights holder. The FIA - the sport's governing body - does formally approve the calendar, but that's essentially a rubber-stamping exercise.

From F1's point of view, primarily it wants the sprints to take place on tracks that will provide an exciting qualifying session and race.

After that, it's about spreading them evenly through the calendar so there are not too many bunched together.

Of course, there are commercial considerations, too. A track has to pay more to host a sprint. But F1 says it would not take the money if it thought it was the wrong place for a sprint.

Then there is the question of the tracks themselves and whether they want a sprint or not. This will be because they feel they can get more spectators through the gate, and/or provide better value for money.

Silverstone managing director Stuart Pringle was keen to have a sprint this year because they want to "deliver as much value as possible for the ticket price", and a sprint means spectators get two races and two qualifying sessions on one weekend.

Pringle said: "We felt it was well worth the additional cost [on the race fee] to give more action."

He pointed out there was a total of 500,000 spectators at the British Grand Prix over the four days in 2025, and 564,000 in 2026.

"The [extra] 64,000 was primarily Friday and Saturday, and we do put that down to the sprint," he said.

Which F1 drivers could consistently challenge for a world title in inferior cars? My wife and I can only come up with four: Ayrton Senna, Michael Schumacher, Fernando Alonso and Max Verstappen. Do you agree? - Martin

It's hard to challenge for a title in an inferior car, and the number of drivers who can do it is limited as a result. Essentially, it is only the very best.

At first glance, your list looks decent, but you have left out two huge names - Lewis Hamilton and Alain Prost.

Prost's most exceptional season was in 1986, when he beat the two Williams drivers - Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet - to win his second world title in what was clearly an inferior McLaren.

There is also a very strong case that Hamilton did not have the best car with McLaren in 2008 (or he and Alonso in 2007), given what was learned subsequently about the relative performance of Ferrari drivers Felipe Massa and Kimi Raikkonen when they were team-mates to Alonso.

The point being that Hamilton and Alonso were extremely closely matched, while Alonso comfortably beat both Massa and Raikkonen, so if Ferrari could compete for a title against McLaren in those years, it could only be because their car was better.

Even in 2017 and 2018, when Hamilton won, the Ferrari was the better car for a large part of both those seasons before Mercedes hit their stride.

The stand-out year relevant to this question is 2012, when Alonso drove his best season and took the title fight to the final race in what was statistically the fourth quickest car.

That was an absolutely extraordinary achievement, and it is rightly celebrated. Even more so when you realise that had only one of two incidents for which Alonso was entirely blameless not happened, he would not have lost out to Red Bull's Sebastian Vettel.

That's a reference, of course, to Alonso being taken out at the start of the Belgian and Japanese Grands Prix by collisions with Lotus drivers - Romain Grosjean in Spa and Raikkonen in Suzuka.

Alonso also arguably won in 2005 in an inferior car, but then it depends what "inferior" means. The Renault was not as fast as Raikkonen's McLaren on balance, but it was certainly more reliable.

As for the rest, no argument with Max Verstappen after coming so close against Lando Norris and McLaren last season, which was Alonso 2012-esque.

Senna won the title in 1991 in a McLaren that was inferior to the Williams FW14 being driven by Mansell, although the Williams suffered significant reliability problems that helped him.

And he also probably did it in 1990 - in his McLaren compared to Prost's Ferrari - given Senna's pace advantage over Prost when they were McLaren team-mates in 1988 and 1989.

Schumacher? Arguably the Benetton was an inferior car to the Williams in 1995, but then he was consistently a superior driver to Damon Hill and David Coulthard, both of whom made a bit of a hash of that season.

Williams also probably had an advantage for the second half of 1994, once they had got on top of the aerodynamic problems that thwarted the start to their season.

But would Schumacher have beaten Senna in 1994 had the Brazilian not been killed at Imola? Unlikely.

And it's hard to argue any of his Ferrari titles were won in an inferior car.

Beyond that, there are not many obvious cases when the champion did not have the best car.

Exceptions would be years massively skewed by circumstance.

One example is the tragic 1982 season, when it was a toss-up between Ferrari and Renault for the fastest car. After Gilles Villeneuve died and team-mate Didier Pironi suffered horrendous injuries, and with Renault afflicted by reliability issues, Keke Rosberg came through to take the title for Williams despite winning only one race.

Or 1979, when the championship scoring system was a bizarre split calculation when only the best four scores from the two half-seasons could be counted, and the Williams FW07 made its debut too late for Alan Jones to challenge Jody Scheckter and Villeneuve in the generally inferior Ferrari 312 T4.

Leonardo Fornaroli looks like another Russell/Leclerc/Piastri calibre driver based on his F3 and F2 performances. If he was to land an F1 seat, where is the most likely place he would end up? - Harry

Fornaroli is the reigning F2 champion, and won F3 the previous season. He has been a member of the McLaren driver development programme since the end of last year.

The Italian has done two practice sessions for McLaren - in Barcelona and Austria this year - as well as two what are known as 'TPC' tests - in older cars - for McLaren in Portimao, and Haas in Jerez.

There are not that many seats up for grabs next year and the driver market is on hold for a large part until it becomes clear whether Max Verstappen is going to leave Red Bull.

If Fornaroli is to get a seat, though, it seems most likely it would be at Haas, where Esteban Ocon's place is under threat.

Haas, however, already have Toyota-contracted Ryo Hirakawa and former Alpine driver Jack Doohan on their books.

Teams always talk about getting "the right balance" of the car. What does that mean specifically, and how do they go about getting it? - Ivor

The car's balance is how a driver experiences its behaviour through a corner.

Does it slide at the front or back (respectively, understeer or oversteer), does it slide differently at different points of the corner, and is the behaviour consistent or unpredictable, etc?

Every driver has their preference as to how they want the car to feel, and the closer the car is to that ideal, generally the quicker they will be.

F1 cars are highly sophisticated prototypes with a number of complex factors affecting how they behave in the cornering phase, which can be broken down into multiple sections making up the time from the moment the driver hits the brakes, to when the car is straight again after the corner.

As a result, there are many different ways in which a car's behaviour can be changed.

These include - but are in no way limited to - the level of downforce chosen at front and rear, the settings for the suspension and differential, and brake pad and disc material.

Drivers can also affect the balance with their driving style. For example, how they enter the corner, when they turn in, how they turn in, how they operate the throttle and brakes on corner entry and so on.
