title: Trump files emergency motion to block BBC from getting financial details about business empire
description: President Trump’s attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust. The British broadcaster received approval from a judge lat...
fullText:
President Trump's attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust.

The British broadcaster received approval from a judge late last month to probe the president's financial documents after Trump claimed he experienced losses due to an episode of the company's "Panorama" series titled "Trump: A Second Chance?"

In the footage, the BBC strung together three separate portions of a speech from Trump to make it look as if he encouraged a violent attack on the Capitol.

"The BBC's improperly broad subpoena demands the Trust's confidential tax, ownership, and financial records for approximately 400 entities," Trump's attorney Alejandro Brito wrote in the legal filing.

"Once the Trust were to begin handing those records over to the BBC, that disclosure could not be undone, and the Trust's pending objections could not restore what the BBC will already have seen," Brito added.

If the emergency motion is not approved, the BBC would be granted insight on Trump's crypto and stock profit, as well as business transactions from at least 400 entities and companies tied to his personal assets managed by family.

Last month, Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett granted the BBC's subpoena to review documents from the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust dating to Jan. 1, 2023.

Her approval requires that the trust start producing documents by Thursday.

"Against the Trust's irreversible injury, the BBC cannot point to any injury, only to brief delay, which does not constitute harm. Fact discovery remains open for months, and the BBC has never explained why it needed a non-party's complete financial records within ten days or how a short stay would impair its defense," Brito wrote.

The BBC has apologized for the documentary edit but has strongly rebuked Trump's push for a payout and attempted to dismiss the lawsuit against the company, arguing U.S. courts hold no legal jurisdiction over the foreign corporation.

The president has refused to back down and recently requested that District Judge Roy Altman allow him to alter the lawsuit in a manner that would shield his financial documents from being reviewed by the British broadcaster.

title: Players who turned World Cup heroics into big transfers
description: BBC Sport looks back at some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned a big transfer.
fullText:
The World Cup is football's biggest stage, filled with goals, drama and unforgettable moments - but it can also prove to be the ultimate shop window.

World Cup heroics have transformed players' lives in the past, and Vozinha's recent move to Chilean side Colo-Colo after an impressive tournament with Cape Verde is the latest reminder that the competition still has the power to change careers.

At the age of 40, the goalkeeper's journey from the Portuguese second division to Chile's biggest club may be unique, but he is not the first to get a big move after starring on the global stage.

Here are some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned them a big move.

Similar to Vozinha, Marc-Vivien Foe was an unknown name before the 1994 World Cup.

Despite Cameroon's disappointing World Cup campaign in the USA, compared to their historic run in 1990, Foe emerged as one of the team's best performers during his debut tournament.

A standout game against Brazil caught attention, which then led to a free transfer from Cameroon's Canon Yaounde to French side Lens.

Foe spent four years at Lens and helped them achieve their first league title in the 1997-98 season.

He also played for West Ham United, Manchester City and Lyon, where he won the French League Cup and Lyon's first Ligue 1 title in 2002.

Foe tragically passed away in June 2003 after he collapsed during a Confederations Cup semi-final against Colombia.

Gilberto Silva's first appearance at a World Cup came in 2002, when the tournament was hosted in South Korea and Japan.

The 25-year-old, who played in Brazil's top division for Atletico Miniero, returned home as a World Cup winner who played every minute of every game for Luiz Felipe Scolari's team.

Silva was only brought into the starting XI because Brazil captain Emerson was ruled out by injury.

But, after playing a key role in Brazil's triumph, the midfielder earned a move to Premier League champions Arsenal.

Nicknamed 'The Invisible Wall', the defensive midfielder joined the Gunners from Atletico Mineiro for about £4.5m.

During his six years in north London, Silva won two FA Cups and played a key role in the famous 2003-04 Invincibles side that went unbeaten to claim the Premier League title.

At the age of 22, Javier Mascherano announced himself on the global stage at the 2006 World Cup, where he helped Argentina reach the quarter-finals.

His performances for both his club back in Brazil and at the World Cup drew the attention of European clubs.

Mascherano initially expressed his desire to remain at Corinthians and help the club in their relegation battle.

However, he soon made the move to West Ham United in the summer of 2006 alongside his Argentina team-mate Carlos Tevez, who also impressed at the World Cup in Germany.

Mascherano had a brief spell with the Hammers until the beginning of 2007, leaving to join Liverpool where he featured in their 2007 Champions League final defeat by AC Milan.

Mascherano then played for Barcelona from 2010, winning the Champions League twice and being part of squads that won La Liga on five occasions.

At the age of just 21, Mesut Ozil emerged as one of the world's most exciting young players after he helped Germany finish third at the 2010 World Cup.

After registering four goals and four assists in seven games, Ozil was able to show off his quality and prove he was a standout performer.

Big clubs took note, and by August 2010, Ozil switched Werder Bremen for Real Madrid, for a fee of about 15m euros (£12.4m).

Copa del Rey, La Liga and Spanish Super Cup titles were to follow during his three year stay in Madrid, before becoming Arsenal's record signing for £42.4m in 2013.

James Rodriguez became one of the stars of the 2014 World Cup, scoring six goals for Colombia and winning the Golden Boot after a memorable run to the quarter-finals.

His excellent performances, including his famous volley against Uruguay, earned him a spot in Fifa's team of the tournament.

The volley against Uruguay was later voted as the best goal in the tournament by more than four million people on Fifa's website and won the Fifa Puskas Award for the best goal of the year.

Real Madrid decided to sign Rodriguez from Monaco for about 75m euros (£71m) after the tournament - a move that led to him winning multiple trophies with Los Blancos, including two Champions Leagues.

Well, you knew this one was coming.

Vozinha became a cult hero when Cape Verde claimed their first World Cup point against Spain in the group stage and his social media fame has exploded from 50,000 Instagram followers to nearly 30 million.

After helping his team reach the knockout stages, taking finalists Argentina to extra time in the last 32, Vozinha was named in Fifa's team of the tournament and even had a newly discovered species of sea slug named after him.

Vozinha's career has taken him to Slovakia, Angola, Moldova, Cyprus and, until recently, Portuguese second division side Chaves, but he has always believed himself to be a "big club player".

Joining Colo Colo, the most successful team in the Primera Division (34 titles) and Copa Chile (14), is his career "highlight".

Gheorghe Hagi - Brescia to Barcelona (1994)

Dejan Stankovic - Red Star Belgrade to Lazio (1998)

Carlos Salcido - Guadalajara to PSV Eindhoven (2006)

Nicolas Otamendi - Velez Sarsfield to Porto (2010)

Edinson Cavani - Palermo to Napoli (2010)

Sami Khedira - Stuttgart to Real Madrid (2010)

Alexis Sanchez - Udinese to Barcelona (2010)

Keylor Navas - Levante to Real Madrid (2014)

Enner Valencia - Pachuca to West Ham United (2014)

title: Lynch exit 'pretty much a snap decision' - O'Doherty
description: Derry City chairman Philip O'Doherty tells BBC Sport NI he thought "it was time to make a change" following news of the departure of manager Tiernan Lynch.
fullText:
Derry City chairman Philip O'Doherty has said that the decision to part ways with manager Tiernan Lynch was one that had only been finally arrived at quite quickly.

The Brandywell club announced the departure of Lynch on Wednesday after a disappointing season to date.

The Candystripes sit sixth in the Premier Division table and have won just one of their past seven games.

The former Larne double title winning boss had been manager of Derry since November 2024 and guided them to a second place finish in the league last season, plus qualification for European competition.

O'Doherty told BBC Sport NI that it was "pretty much a snap decision" to part company with Lynch, with it only being finalised on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.

"He [Lynch] had a really good season last year, this year hasn't been up to expectations and has been a disappointment," O'Doherty told BBC Sport NI.

"We've assembled a reasonably good squad we think, and it's getting better with the arrival of Mark Connolly in a director of football role, but I just thought if we were going to make a change now was the right time to do it.

"We've got all to fight for in terms of European spaces and we're still in the cup."

Pressure had been building on Lynch in recent months in light of poor results, with some supporters vocal in calling for a change.

"I don't follow social media and I don't follow a lot of the football pundits either. I look at what's happening on the field and speak to my fellow directors and we make a decision, and we thought it was time," explained the Derry chairman.

"The players weren't expecting it and were probably thinking we will fight through the rest of the season but by and large they understand it.

"He [Tiernan] was disappointed but we shook hands and I wished him the best of luck."

Former club captain and recently appointed director of football Connolly has been named interim manager at the club.

"He [Connolly] knows the squad of players, he lives in Derry, which is very important. Mark was part of the team, he was the captain of the team that got second place last year and he came in as director of football," added O'Doherty.

"Mark would have a lot of respect from those players. Bringing anybody new in was probably going to be difficult anyway.

"I think Mark fits the bill. He's a young manager and I think it will take a little bit of help from the senior players in particular. Michael Duffy is the captain but we will probably need four or five captains because he lacks experience in managing.

"But he has shown all the right qualities so far and he's certainly a man motivator. I just think it's a challenge that he'll rise to and he certainly made himself available once the question was asked."

Club captain Michael Duffy said the players were told the news of Lynch's departure after training and described it as "a difficult day".

"You don't like to see anyone losing their job but it is what it is. As players we move on and try and get three points on Friday. We know we haven't been good enough this year.

"I played with Mark and he's a real leader. He knows football, he knows this group and he knows a lot of the players."

Derry are at home to Sligo Rovers in their next league fixture on Friday night, a game which will be streamed live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website.

"We need to go and play with confidence and build on what we've been doing the past few weeks.

"We need to finish strongly, climb up that table and try to catch that European spot and try to win that cup," Duffy added.

title: How Buttler became T20 cricket's run-scoring GOAT
description: BBC Sport explores how Jos Buttler became the highest run-getter in men's T20 cricket.
fullText:
He did it with a six, of course.

Jos Buttler thrashed Marco Jansen's ball over square leg and on to the balcony of the hotel behind the stand at Old Trafford.

That shot helped the England white-ball great move to 14,833 runs in T20 cricket, surpassing Kieron Pollard's mark of 14,803 to become the highest run-scorer in the format's history.

The Manchester Super Giants number three went on to make 51 from 20 balls, another superb innings in a remarkable 522-match career in the sport's shortest format.

The 35-year-old is in a sparkling run of form in T20s, making 50+ scores in three of his last four Hundred matches - which count towards T20 stats - and hammering a 64-ball 131 in his most recent international outing, a victory over India at Southampton last month.

BBC Sport takes a look at the statistics that put the former England white-ball captain among the greats of the T20 game, and the reasons behind his remarkable longevity.

The race, whether stated or not, has been on since 2022.

That was when Chris Gayle, the charismatic West Indies opener who blazed a trail in the shortest format, played his last professional game, setting a mark of 14,562 runs in T20 cricket.

Buttler was always one of the leading candidates to take the record down.

However, it was another West Indian in T20 journeyman Pollard, 39, who beat him to it, passing Gayle's total in June and extending the record to 14,803 over the course of the Major League Cricket season.

Pollard had the advantage as the leading appearance maker in the format with 741 - 139 more than Sunil Narine in second place.

Buttler sits ninth on that list with 522 appearances and while he is England's highest T20 appearance maker with 160 caps, he doesn't hold the record for most appearances in the format by an Englishman.

That goes to Alex Hales, who has made 528 appearances and was another candidate to break the record - he has 14,429 runs to his name and sits fourth in the all-time list.

Buttler's total includes 1,192 runs scored in 31 matches in The Hundred, with cricket statisticians including data from the competition in T20 records.

It all started in Hyderabad, curiously enough.

Playing in the short-lived Champions League Twenty20 in 2009, Somerset debutant Buttler, who had recently turned 19, emerged at number nine against New South Wales.

A single driven down the ground off Moises Henriques was the first of six runs that day, finishing unbeaten as his side closed on 111 and then lost the match within 12 overs.

When he made his England debut, almost two years later in Manchester, he wasn't called upon to bat as the home side beat India. Indeed, he didn't bat in three of his first four T20I appearances.

Buttler's first taste of life in international cricket was as a lower-order finisher, and his first runs for England in that India series were 13 from number seven.

He started slowly, with an unbeaten 32 against South Africa - his one score higher than 15 in his first 11 innings at international level.

However, former England team-mate Dawid Malan said Buttler's qualities were always evident.

"He started young [he was 20 when he made his England debut]. He always had the scoops and power and he's developed with the modern game," said Malan.

"He's never been left behind and he's almost been at the forefront of pushing the modern game and what players can do."

Buttler's first half-century for England came against New Zealand in 2013, though it took until the 2021 T20 World Cup for his first ton - against Sri Lanka in Sharjah, off 67 balls.

While Buttler has been remarkably consistent in the format - he has averaged fewer than 30 in just one of the past 12 calendar years (2017) - he has really kicked on since 2021, a period which has brought all nine of his T20 tons.

Having emerged as a late-order hitter, his run-scoring became even more prolific when he moved up the order to open the batting for his respective teams.

His record in the powerplay is superb, with an average of 43 in the first six overs of the innings and, of all the English batters to have more than 1,000 powerplay runs in the format, only two better Buttler's average, albeit having played considerably less cricket (Tom Westley and Kevin Pietersen).

And if he's still around during the death overs, Buttler is even more destructive - striking at 184 between overs 16 and 20 compared to 143 at the top of the innings.

It is all based around some very simple principles.

"Jos Buttler's whole philosophy is to hit the ball on the off side," said Malan.

"When you speak to him about batting he is very big on looking off side and, at the death in particular, he's always looking to hit the sightscreen flat. That is weird because generally players are trying to hit the ball high and out of the ground.

"But by doing that [looking to hit the sightscreen flat] he is pushing his left hip at the bowler. He has two things he believes in; hitting the sightscreen and doing that. He gets himself into positions where he's so strong with his base that he can find the ball with his hands."

Ex-England paceman Steven Finn pointed to Buttler's wristy style of play as he added: "The first time I bowled at him in the nets, the ball just made a different sound of his bat.

"The way he turns his wrists and hockey slaps it when he hits a cover drive or when he hits a six down the ground, he's got such strong wrists which I think makes him a bit different to other batters who are more classical with the way they hit the ball."

It is a technique honed in all forms of cricket at the highest level.

"One of the things that people forget is Jos Buttler played 57 Tests for England," said Malan. "He learned his batsmanship through that and learned how to build an innings and how to win games of cricket.

"That education, mixed with his power, means he's able to transfer that to his white-ball cricket."

Perhaps Buttler's greatest strength is his lack of weakness against any particular form of bowling.

Against seam from either hand and versus off-break and slow left-arm spin, the difference in his average is within a margin of a run, sitting between 37 and 38.

Only against leg-break bowling does his average tail off a little, but only to a still respectable 31.31, while he is prolific against the uncommon left-arm unorthodox spin, averaging 48.20.

His boundary ball percentage is marginally better against seam, sitting in the low 20s as opposed to the mid-teens against spin.

His strike-rate is best against the right-arm seamers, against whom he has scored almost 50% of his runs - reflective of the type of bowlers he faces in the powerplay.

Buttler is particularly dismissive of the short ball - averaging 74 against it since 2021 - while of players to have more than 500 runs in the same period, only Pakistan's Mohammad Rizwan averages more against short-pitched bowling.

It's quite staggering that fellow white-ball legends Trent Boult, Matt Henry and Sam Curran have never dismissed Buttler in T20 cricket and only two men have got the better of him more than five times - India duo Bhuvneshwar Kumar and Varun Chakaravarthy.

Afghanistan's Rashid Khan has the best strike-rate against Buttler - removing him six times in just 82 deliveries.

"He's captained and played all around the world and he's been a marquee player," said Malan.

"When you are the marquee player in the team, you get paid the most and the expectation from the owners, captains, coaches and team-mates is that you're going to go out and score runs every single time - and the pressure that comes with that is immense.

"His whole life, he's been able to deal with pressure. That just makes it all the more remarkable what he's done."

Buttler turns 36 on 8 September, and will be 38 by the time the next edition of the T20 World Cup arrives in late 2028.

Of the ICC full members, only Afghanistan carried a player of that age in the 2026 competition, but Buttler has shown few signs of decline and is likely to be part of England's party travelling to Australia and New Zealand.

He struggled in the World Cup earlier this year, averaging 10.87 from eight matches, but with the tournament returning to the grounds where Buttler led his country to victory in 2022, don't count against him lifting the trophy for a second time.

title: Ex-England prop Marler to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
description: The former rugby star will be known as Mauler when the fourth series airs in 2027, the BBC confirmed.
fullText:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in battle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.

title: Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes
description: With Bruno Guimaraes set to sign for Premier League champions Arsenal, BBC Sport look at why the Gunners wanted the Newcastle skipper.
fullText:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made clear in the immediate aftermath of the Gunners' Premier League title win that they would need to be ambitious to build on their success - and the club have backed him with the move to sign Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes.

Arsenal won the league for the first time in 22 years last season and reached the Champions League final where they were beaten by Paris St-Germain.

But as soon as the curtain came down on that campaign and the parade to celebrate their new silverware had finished, Arteta's thoughts moved to taking Arsenal to a "different dimension".

And with Brazil's Guimaraes set to be part of a new-look Arsenal midfield, the club believe they are signing a player who will do exactly that.

Arteta has always been keen on signing players with Premier League experience and who have shown they can operate with the demands at the highest level.

And with the addition of the 28-year-old, the club's aim of creating one of the best midfields in world football is a step closer.

There are a number of reasons why Guimaraes was the player Arteta decided can ensure Arsenal are ready to fight on multiple fronts.

The Gunners were plagued with injuries last season and, despite a £250m spend in the last summer transfer window, a player's robustness has always been considered when making signings.

Arsenal played 63 games in all competitions last season and have revamped their medical department before the new campaign.

Christian Norgaard, who is set to move to Everton, was brought in last summer but was not trusted by Arteta and was limited to just seven appearances and one start in the league last season.

That put heavy demands on Martin Zubimendi and Declan Rice, with the former dropping out of the side completely as the amount of work he was asked to do took its toll during the run-in.

Rice is coming back from a World Cup campaign where he helped England reach the semi-finals after a season in which he played the most minutes of any outfield player at Arsenal.

Rice has been carrying a hamstring issue but rest is expected to have helped to ease the problem, with Guimaraes' addition ensuring there will be no dip in quality if Arteta rotates his starting XI, while the ceiling of the midfield is raised too.

Arteta is known for demanding intensity in training and with Guimaraes set to join a midfield stocked with Rice, Zubimendi, captain Martin Odegaard, Eberechi Eze, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ethan Nwaneri, there will be no shortage of competition.

Arsenal have a leadership group that supports club captain Odegaard but, with the addition of Guimaraes, they will be bringing in a player who is a natural leader.

Guimaraes became Newcastle's talisman during his time at St James' Park and, as Arteta looks to maximise every marginal gain he can, the Brazilian's ability and his way of connecting with supporters will be another weapon.

Arsenal have had campaigns seriously affected by injury, but Guimaraes has missed just 16 Premier League games since he signed for Newcastle in 2022.

And his impact is backed up by the fact Newcastle's win percentage (12.5%), points per game (0.7), average goals for (0.8) and even average goals against (1.6) all suffer in the top flight when he is not available.

Although it is an admittedly larger sample size, Opta data shows that Newcastle's win percentage (50.7%), points per game (1.7), average goals for (1.9) and average goals against (1.3) have been significantly higher when Guimaraes has featured.

Guimaraes was Newcastle's top scorer in the league last season with nine goals and he provided four assists for Brazil at the World Cup in his five starts.

Despite missing six games with hamstring injury towards the end of last season, Guimaraes still ranked in the top five players across the league for defensive line-breaking passes (46) and through balls (21).

He also led the way at Newcastle for passes under high intensity pressure (998), which illustrates how he relishes responsibility.

Staff at Newcastle have called him an "inspirational" figure and Arsenal and Arteta will be hoping he can produce the same feeling at Emirates Stadium.

title: Why Liverpool are ready to make Barcola third £100m signing
description: With Liverpool prepared to make Bradley Barcola their third £100m signing, BBC Sport looks at what the France and Paris St-Germain winger would bring to Anfield.
fullText:
Liverpool have twice paid more than £100m for players - midfielder Florian Wirtz and striker Alexander Isak - and could be about to pay that much once again.

Paris St-Germain and France winger Bradley Barcola has become a main target for Liverpool, with the Reds prepared to pay about £100m, while PSG are holding out for somewhere near £145m.

Liverpool, who finished fifth in the Premier League last season, 25 points behind champions Arsenal, could eventually end up paying Bayer Leverkusen £116m for Wirtz, while they shelled out a club record £125m to sign Isak from Newcastle in September.

And they could be about to break the bank yet again to bring in 23-year-old Barcola, who was part of France's squad at the World Cup.

He came on as a second-half substitute in both the past two Champions League finals, when PSG beat Inter Milan 5-0 in 2024-25 and then in May when they edged past Arsenal on penalties to retain their title.

Barcola moved to PSG from Lyon in 2023 for a reported £38.5m and has since also won three Ligue 1 titles, the French Cup twice, as well as the Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Intercontinental Cup.

He is right footed, although he prefers to play on the left wing, but can also play on the right or through the middle.

However, with PSG also having Georgia's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and France's Desire Doue as wide options, Barcola does not play 90 minutes every match so a move to Anfield would give him more playing time.

With Mohamed Salah leaving on a free transfer at the end of last season having scored 257 goals in a hugely successful nine-year spell with the Reds, Liverpool clearly need to strengthen their attack.

France forward Hugo Ekitike ruptured his Achilles tendon in April and is not expected to play again in 2026, while Cody Gakpo, another who can play on the left and in the middle, has been linked with a move to Tottenham, although Liverpool say they do not want to sell.

The Reds' other current attacking options include 17-year-old Rio Ngumoha, Italy forward Federico Chiesa and new signing Victor Munoz.

Barcola has played 28 times for France and scored three goals in this summer's World Cup, including in the 6-4 loss to England in the third-place play-off.

However, like at club level, his game time was limited because of the skills of his 21-year-old PSG team-mate Doue.

Boss Didier Deschamps stuck with Ballon d'Or holder Ousmane Dembele on the right and rotated Barcola and Doue, with both men starting four of France's eight World Cup matches, but never in the same game.

At first glance, Barcola looks like the natural successor to Luis Diaz.

Liverpool chose not to sign a direct replacement after the Colombian's departure last summer, but the underlying data suggests the PSG forward could fill that void.

Opta's player similarity model rates the Frenchman as the winger whose output most closely resembled Diaz's across Europe's top five leagues in 2025-26 (78%), with Mohamed Salah (65%), Lamine Yamal (61%) and Vinicius Junior (61%) the next closest matches.

A closer look, however, suggests Liverpool would not simply be replacing one winger with another.

Barcola is a left winger by trade, having played almost all of his Champions League minutes for PSG on that flank, but his game is shaped by a centre-forward's instincts. He played as a striker until the age of 17, something reflected in his movement and shot selection.

Last season, he averaged 3.5 shots per 90 minutes in Ligue 1, placing him among the division's most active shooters despite operating from wide areas.

His 9.83 expected goals (xG) ranked in the 95th percentile among wingers across Europe's top five leagues, meaning only around 5% of wide players consistently found themselves in better goalscoring positions.

Barcola converted those chances into 11 league goals, outperforming his xG, while no PSG player or Ligue 1 winger recorded a higher xG total during the 2025-26 campaign.

Those instincts are reflected in how he attacks defenders. Barcola was the only player across Europe's top five leagues to average more than two shot-ending carries per 90 minutes (2.06), illustrating his ability to drive at opponents before creating shooting opportunities for himself.

He also averaged 8.69 touches in the opposition penalty area per 90 minutes - the seventh-highest figure among more than 1,500 eligible players - reinforcing the profile of a winger who consistently occupies goalscoring positions.

His shot map highlights a player who attacks dangerous central areas rather than settling for speculative efforts from distance. Only Ousmane Dembele had a better combined shot volume with chance creation in Ligue 1, underlining Barcola's rare ability to both finish attacks and create opportunities for team-mates.

The comparison with Salah is equally revealing. While both pose a significant goal threat, Barcola is a more direct ball carrier.

He attempted more take-ons per 90 than the Egypt forward last season (4.26 to 3.38), but created fewer chances (2.16 to 2.33), attempted far fewer crosses (1.15 to 4.89) and through balls (0.25 to 0.59).

The numbers point towards a player who looks to eliminate defenders himself rather than orchestrate attacks from wide areas.

There are also signs that his game continues to evolve under Luis Enrique.

Barcola's passing profile across his three Champions League campaigns at PSG has become increasingly focused on progressing play in the final third, reflecting greater tactical maturity.

Rather than dribbling at every opportunity, he now shows a better understanding of when to accelerate attacks and when to recycle possession.

His work without the ball is another reason Liverpool's recruitment team are understood to admire him. Barcola ranked ninth across Europe's top five leagues for possessions won in the final third last season, a metric that reflects the aggressive pressing and intensity likely to be demanded under Andoni Iraola.

That profile may suit Liverpool's evolving attack. With Wirtz excelling at releasing runners between the lines, and Ekitike and Isak expected to occupy central defenders, Liverpool arguably need another player capable of attacking space rather than demanding the ball to feet.

Barcola's willingness to make penetrative runs and arrive in goalscoring positions could provide exactly that.

Perhaps most encouragingly for any prospective buyer, there is reason to believe Barcola has not yet reached his ceiling.

A late physical developer, he has already transformed from a promising Lyon academy graduate into a two-time Champions League winner with PSG.

At just 23, his blend of pace, intelligent movement, elite shot volume, relentless pressing and growing creative output suggests one of Europe's most complete young wide forwards is still improving.

Liverpool ship four second-half goals to leave Iraola with much to ponder

John: Truly flabbergasted at his price. Not denying his quality and potential but when you hear Vinicius Jr is valued at £137m you have to give your head a scratch.

Lee: He's proved his worth. A big signing for the new manager makes sense, get the season started with a buzz. Realistically we still need to look at the back four conundrum though.

Stu: Barcola would be a good signing but he's not worth anywhere near £100m, never mind £145m. He's a squad player at PSG. If they won't accept £70m max then move on to someone else.

Andrew: Ridiculous amount of money. Can Barcola actually last a full 90 minutes? He seemed to be subbed between 60 and 70 mins. I hope that proves to be wrong if we buy him.

Paul: There appears to be enough attacking options already, surely last year showed the need is in defence. Make the backline solid and build out from there.

title: What did Premiership start tell us about Scottish sides' Euro hopes?
description: With Rangers, Hearts, Hibernian and Motherwell in action on Thursday, BBC Scotland has been attempting to analyse the chances of the nation's European hopefuls.
fullText:
As the dust settles on a blockbuster opening weekend of the new Scottish Premiership season, fans of Scotland's European representatives have food for thought after seeing their sides in domestic action for the first time this term.

Supporters have been left pondering whether their teams are undercooked, oven-ready or some other cooking-related adjective you can think of.

Given the stage of summer at which the Premiership returns, the answer is regularly the former, but what did the first round of fixtures tell us?

While Celtic have to wait a fortnight for their Champions League play-off, Rangers, Hearts, Hibernian and Motherwell are in European qualifying action on Thursday.

Celtic drawn against LASK as other Scottish sides discover opponents

Podcast: Which Scottish side has toughest route in Europe?

How Johansson is rising to daunting Motherwell challenge

Same start but different outlook at Rangers as McInnes era begins

As the team with the second-highest coefficient ranking in the whole of Europa League qualifying behind Benfica, who play Hearts in their third-round qualifier, Rangers should be confident of making it through against Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Derek McInnes' men are away in Thursday's first leg (17:00 BST) in Poland against a side who, like Rangers, finished third in their domestic league last term.

However, Jagiellonia's recent European history is a warning to anyone assuming Rangers will progress to the play-off round to face either Northern Irish champions Larne or Iberia Tbilisi of Georgia.

Jagiellonia, who have won their opening two domestic league games, have reached the knockout phase of the Conference League in the past two seasons.

They ran Real Betis close in the quarter-finals in 2024-25 and were eliminated in extra time by Fiorentina in the knockout play-off round last term.

Light on centre-backs following an injury to Ben Godfrey, while in-demand John Souttar is not included in their European squad, Rangers head to Poland with issues to iron out after failing to win their opening Premiership match for the fourth straight campaign.

McInnes' side responded to going a goal behind at Dundee United with an improved second-half display to earn a point, but there are concerns, voiced by former midfielder Andy Halliday, about a lack of creativity in the team.

The Ibrox club appear to be attempting to address that with the reported imminent arrival of Hannover's Daisuke Yokota and by entering a transfer tussle with rivals Celtic for Frosinone winger Fares Ghedjemis.

You take over at a club who were denied a historic league title in the final 10 minutes of last season. They then lose their captain and talismanic striker, plus their best midfielder, and have a huge turnover of players.

Your first competitive action is a Champions League qualifier against seasoned European campaigners Sturm Graz, losing 6-0 on aggregate, before conceding twice after the 90th minute up at Aberdeen to lose your first league match.

So, what's next? Benfica in Europa League qualifying. A doddle.

The Portuguese giants await on Thursday (20:00 BST) amid a savage introduction for Hearts' new Belgian head coach. Chances of progression feel slim.

There have been aspects of each of the three matches under Vrancken that have been encouraging, and a win at Pittodrie on Saturday would have been a huge morale boost.

However, the nature of the team's late collapse has intensified fear among the support that their season could unravel before it has even properly started.

A trip to Lisbon to face Marco Silva's Benfica presents a glamour tie but also the prospect of another chastening defeat on the continent as Vrancken tries to piece together his best XI.

The 38-time Portuguese champions beat Napoli and Real Madrid at home in the Champions League last term on their way to the knockout stage, where they were put out by Real, who have since taken head coach Jose Mourinho.

Benfica's domestic action is yet to return after they finished third in the league last season, but they defeated Swiss side St Gallen over two legs to reach this stage of Europa League qualifying.

A 2-1 defeat in Switzerland was wiped out with a thumping 5-0 win in the second leg last Thursday, with four of the five goals coming from Greece striker Vangelis Pavlidis.

After a humiliating first-leg loss to Kosovan minnows Malisheva in Conference League qualifying, Hibs looked to have put an embarrassing night behind them when they went on to win the return leg 4-1 at Easter Road last week.

But defeat to fellow European hopefuls Motherwell on Sunday served them another reality check as they prepare to host Shkendija of North Macedonia on Thursday (20:00 BST).

Shkendija, who played in the Conference League proper last term, progressing to the first knockout round before being beaten heavily over two legs by Turkish club Samsunspor, are a step up from Malisheva.

You just do not know what you are going to get from David Gray's men, who could not take advantage of the pressure they were piling on Motherwell before being stunned by an excellent counter-attack in the closing minutes.

Based on the small amount of evidence under Alfred Johansson, Motherwell arguably look in the best shape of all of Scotland's European representatives.

Many were expecting a natural regression, but the transition from Jens Berthel Askou to his Swedish successor has appeared seamless, despite losing key players.

The Fir Park side made light work of Faroese outfit HB Torshavn before their victory at Easter Road on Sunday, and the only goal they have conceded in 270 minutes of football was a Martin Boyle penalty.

The first of two legs against HJK takes place in Finland on Thursday (17:00 BST). The Helsinki-based team lost 3-0 in their domestic league to SJK on Monday after resting several players, including former Norwich City striker Teemu Pukki.

title: 'Most exciting player' Eala shows 'Filipino heart' to make history
description: After making history in Washington, BBC Sport looks at Alexandra Eala's journey to her first title.
fullText:
As the umpire called the winning point, Alexandra Eala collapsed to the ground in tears - knowing her country had been with her for every step of the tournament.

She overcame weather delays, and the loss of the first set, to defeat world number three Jessica Pegula in the Washington Open final, becoming the first Filipina to win a WTA title.

"To the Filipino community, here in DC and back home, wherever you are in the world. I really feel all the love."

Even Pegula was impressed by the turnout on Monday, for the continuation of Sunday's final.

"I can definitely confirm this is the best Monday final crowd I've seen," the American said. "I'm sure some people took off work. I won't tell them where you guys were."

Former world number one Rafael Nadal, whose academy Eala graduated from, congratulated her on the win, writing on X: "A well-deserved title for all the hard work."

Despite only being 21 years old, this has been a long time coming for Eala.

She first started playing at the age of four, saying: "I went to train every day after school with my ruffled socks, light-up shoes and chubby cheeks."

Going on to join Nadal's tennis academy, she had the opportunity to train with the 22-time Grand Slam champion.

She graduated from there in 2023, having her diploma presented to her by the world number one at the time, Iga Swiatek.

Three years later, Eala knocked the Pole out of Wimbledon - becoming the first player from the Philippines to reach the fourth round of a Grand Slam in the Open era.

Her improvement has been visible, beating the top three seeds at the Washington Open.

After defeating third seed Naomi Osaka, Pegula described the world number 20 as "the future of the tour".

In 2022, Eala was on the cover of Vogue Philippines after becoming the first Filipina to win a junior Grand Slam title.

But it was her victory over Swiatek in the quarter-finals of the Miami Open in 2025, that brought a new passion for tennis to the Philippines.

There has been a lot of love for the young star from her community, with queues to see her play growing and fans following her all over the world.

There are more than 75,000 members of the Filipino community in Washington, with a further four million across the US who will be watching her in the US Open in late August.

"To all the Filipino fans that came out and have supported, you guys are helping grow tennis around the world," Pegula said after the match.

Fellow Filipino and former boxing champion, Manny Pacquiao, wrote on social media that her comeback showed the "heart of a Filipino" before calling her "our new champion".

Former British number one Greg Rusedski has hailed Eala as "the most exciting player on the WTA Tour".

"She is fearless, she takes the ball early, she is a lefty," he said on his podcast Off Court With Greg Rusedski. "Her mentality is so good and so strong."

"The one area she needs in her game to win a major is to get that serve a bit better and more powerful.

"Maybe next year if she can get that improvement on the serve then she's definitely in the mix [for a major] because the rest of her game is there."

US Open champion and former world number one Andy Roddick described her as "the real deal".

"She is just not scared to go against the top players," he said.

"For some reason what she does with switching directions and accepting pace and pinning people in corners, she is a name nobody wants to see early in a draw as a top player."

title: The summer that changed Welsh football
description: A decade on from Euro 2016, key figures tell BBC Sport Wales the inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football forever.
fullText:
"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open – his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley – to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there – and that stems from 2016.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 – a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

title: Why we are still waiting for the 'Newey effect' - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
fullText:
Formula 1 is now on it summer break before the season resumes with the Dutch Grand Prix, from 21-23 August.

However, BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson is still here to answer your latest questions.

The new Aston Martin package has undoubtedly been a success, but they are still well below expectations. Should we have already seen the 'Newey effect', and if so, why has the designer who is repeatedly described as 'the best' not had the expected impact? - Benjamin

There are logical reasons why the Aston Martin-Honda package - so strong on paper - has not yet come together.

In short, the new 2026 aerodynamic regulations were published on 2 January 2025. But Adrian Newey did not start officially at Aston Martin in his new role as managing technical partner until 2 March.

When he arrived, he asked the team to stop what they had already worked on and switch to his design outline. That put them two months behind already.

Then, the wind tunnel was not ready to receive any modelling until mid-April, so now they were nearly four months behind the others.

On top of that, the team only realised in November last year that Honda was a long way behind on its engine design.

The cumulative effect of all this was seen at the start of the year, when it became obvious the car and the engine were both uncompetitive and unreliable.

In the intervening period, Aston Martin, as Newey put it, "overhauled how we work", improved organisation, put in place different systems, and rethought the car.

The result was the car that made its debut in Hungary, which was significantly lighter and had much improved downforce. It cut lap times by about two seconds, it seems.

The first upgrade of the Honda engine comes at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break, which is expected to reduce some - but by no means all, or even the majority - of the gap to the leading engines.

All of that means it will be 2027 before the first full-fat Newey-led design appears. And its competitiveness will also depend on how Honda gets on with its 2027 engine.

With the sudden arrival of Malaysia on the calendar, how do the drivers, especially those who haven't raced there, prepare for the race? - Jacob

The Malaysian Grand Prix was always renowned as one of the toughest on the calendar, because of the demands placed on the body by the tropical conditions.

But the same goes for Singapore, which was already on the calendar and which is just a week after Malaysia on the latest schedule.

So the drivers will not need to do anything different in their preparations than they would already be doing for Singapore - they often say that the training they do all year is focused on being able to cope with the humidity and heat there.

One problem the introduction of Malaysia does pose, however, is time zones.

For Singapore, the drivers and teams essentially stay on European time, because of the night-race schedule. So, getting up around lunchtime, going to bed around 3-5am.

But Malaysia is a daytime race, so they will have to switch to local time for that one, having been in Azerbaijan the previous weekend, and then migrate back towards European time for Singapore.

However, these are world-class athletes who are used to this sort of thing, so they will be fine.

Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season

If, as looks likely, the F1 season might finish in Europe (probably Italy), will the low temperatures make the race a bit processional with the low temperatures providing low grip? Is there not a better solution available somewhere warmer, South Africa, Portugal or Thailand for instance? - Alan

The end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are in doubt because of the ongoing war between the US/Israel and Iran.

If the situation does not improve by the time F1 has to make a decision, which F1 president Stefano Domenicali says is mid-September, then the races will have to be cancelled.

At the moment, the most likely solution is a race in Imola in Italy in early December.

The weather in Italy at that time can be cold, of course. But, as Domenicali pointed out on a call with F1 media last week, perhaps not as cold as in Las Vegas at the end of November.

It gets pretty chilly at night in Las Vegas when the grand prix is on, and the track surface there is especially non-abrasive. And of course, as it's a night race, there is no solar radiation to heat up the track surface, which there would be to some degree in Imola.

So if the tyres can cope with Las Vegas, they can cope with Imola.

Why not somewhere warmer? As ever in F1, the sport does not just put on a race for the sake of there being a race, it also has to make financial and logistical sense.

You say Thailand - there is no track there. South Africa? It has Kyalami, but F1 has been trying to stage a race in Africa for some years but it proved impossible for various reasons in South Africa.

Portugal's Portimao is back on the calendar for real in 2027, but construction work needs to be done for it to be ready, and it could not do that and host a race in December.

The same goes for Istanbul Park, where the weather in December may well be no better than Imola.

And there is also all the travel-related documentation to consider.

Domenicali said last week: "Considering the constraint that we have, we need to go back to close all the Brexit-connected documentation from abroad in the UK and then go to another place.

"Therefore, the only possibility is to finish in Europe within the same framework of the time, hoping that there will be no snow, as we can hope in other places."

There seem to be more significant upgrades from a number of teams this year, McLaren's being the latest. Will the top four teams be bringing many 

All the F1 teams headed into 2026 knowing that the season would be defined by development.

When there is a new rule set, this is always the case. The longer a set of rules exists, the more a) the car designs converge; b) teams get into diminishing returns.

But at the start, progress comes faster and in bigger steps, and that explains the fluctuation in form between the top teams so far this season.

Typically, a team will bring an upgrade, their competitiveness will increase, but then it will shift as other teams bring their own upgrades.

The longer a team leaves it between upgrades, the more they fall back.

That's why McLaren, for example, made a leap forward with their Miami upgrade, but slowly slipped back as Mercedes and Ferrari brought their own big developments in Canada and Spain.

Then, McLaren leapt forwards - even more than they expected - with their Hungary upgrade. And they have another due in Zandvoort. And more to come after that.

Ferrari, Mercedes and Red Bull also have developments to come after the summer break.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said in Hungary: "I still believe that if we want to be in a position to fight for victories consistently in the future, we need to keep our focus on delivering more upgrades. That is the plan, but we are not naive. We know that this will be the plan for all the teams.

"Like it's always been in this 2026 season, it's a matter of a race of upgrades. And the good news is that McLaren is now back in this race of upgrades while fighting for the lead.

"But I expect that the car that will be the best car at the end of the season will keep adding tenths of a second in the next 11 races, probably as much as half a second. So definitely a lot of work ahead of everyone, not only McLaren."

The limiting factor is the cost cap - all teams are restricted to spending no more than $215m on racing and development this season.

This means teams have to be strategic in how they deploy their new parts, "rather than just throwing it in at every grand prix, like in the past", as Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff put it in Hungary.

He added: "We're bringing upgrades, we're closely monitoring how much we can bring. At the moment, cost cap-wise, we're in a good spot. We've tried to have it a little bit more second-half-of-the-season weighted, and we'll see if that's enough."

Why don't McLaren make their own engines? They often seem to struggle because they rely on others' (Mercedes) power units, who are also a direct competitor. Surely McLaren have the expertise and they could benefit their road car industry and their F1 car if they became a works team. - Jack

Making a Formula 1 engine is a highly specialised enterprise. It's also extremely expensive. The manufacturers supplying engines to F1 this year have all spent hundreds of millions of pounds developing their power-units.

Apart from Red Bull, all are car manufacturers who have wider automotive companies to offset the cost, and expertise on which to lean.

There is now an engine budget cap, set at $190m in a company's inaugural year, and $148.5m after that.

McLaren is a road-car manufacturer. But it does not build engines. It outsources its engines to a UK company called Ricardo.

The plans for the next F1 engine, due in either 2030 or 2031, are still being formalised, and there is considerable debate about them.

However, one aspect all stakeholders are agreed upon is for the costs to come down, perhaps even to the point where becoming a supplier of customer engines becomes a viable business proposition, which is not the case at the moment.

McLaren have proved they can win titles as a customer team, but they have also had frustrations with their Mercedes relationship this year. They have discovered how customer teams are on the back foot when it comes to maximising the operations of such complex engines at the start of a new regulation cycle.

As for the future, McLaren Racing chief executive officer Zak Brown said at the Monaco Grand Prix: "Priority one is to stay with Mercedes. They've been a great partner. Any time a new regulation comes out, we'll take a look and see, is it something technically that's interesting? Is it something fiscally that makes sense?

"We'll go through that process when that happens. But sitting here right now, we're extremely happy with Mercedes and we anticipate continuing with them."

F1 Drivers As Teletubbies?! F1’s Silly Season Is Here!

title: Analysis: Trump fumes as top allies back down on his personal battles
description: A president used to bending US politics to his will faces two stinging losses in a matter of days, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher.
fullText:
Watch: "She folded like an umbrella" - Trump attacks Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool

It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of contravening evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted – what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury – provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he groused.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

'She folded like an umbrella' - Trump slams Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool case

Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs

One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

Holdout senators back Blanche for AG after he formally withdraws Trump fund plan

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

Trump on Blanche: "He's going to do a great job"

While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public.

That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action.

On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations.

"They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote.

If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time – but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough.

The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals.

Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history.

Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity.

"My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday.

In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers.

While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventially face.
